# did:guardian -- full text
This file concatenates every page under /docs/ in full, for a single-fetch read. Each section below corresponds to one live page; the canonical URL for each is given in its own heading.

# did:guardian

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/

**did:guardian is a distributed identity built around the concept of guardianship.** In most identity systems, control lives in a single keypair, and losing it means losing the identity for good. A did:guardian identity can have a group of guardians, which are other identities that have the power to recover it or deactivate it. Guardianship is optional, and its exact rules for how the guardianship works are set by the identity's owner in advance.

## Why this exists

Three situations come up often enough to need a standard answer:


**You lose access to your own identity.** A lost device, a forgotten key, a compromised laptop. Most identity systems have no support path for this, or have minimal support via recovery keys. Fundamentally, the key is the identity, and no key means no identity. `did:guardian` lets you name people (or other identities) in advance who can jointly restore access, the same way a family member could help you recover a bank account, but can't spend the money in it.



**Someone needs standing authority to act for an identity.** The word "guardian" comes from family law, where a guardian makes important decisions (e.g. medical, financial, legal), for someone who can't make them for themselves. did:guardian carries that same idea into a digital identity. A company might not want the AI agent it runs to have full authority over certain actions on its own. Its guardian can act on its behalf for those specific actions instead, via the reference registrar's own [delegation-chain token exchange](/docs/registrar/#10-delegation-chain-tokens-token-exchange) -- a registrar-profile mechanism, not something the method itself defines a dedicated operation for. Acting on an identity's behalf this way is one of guardianship's primary uses.



**Responsibility for an identity needs to change hands.** A board member's term ends. A shared agent gets reassigned to a new team, or the team membership changes. did:guardian treats adding and removing a guardian as its own signed, auditable operation.


## How it works


By default, a `did:guardian` identity functions no differently than a standard DID, controlling its keys directly. However, an identity can optionally have one or more **guardians**, becoming a **ward** of those guardians. Guardians are other identities (people, organizations, or other wards) granted the power to recover it, deactivate it, or act on its behalf, under a policy that any verifier checks by replaying the log.

A simple example of this is a human that manages an agent. The agent has a fully functional id, and the human has a separate id, but the human can be assigned as the agent's *guardian*.


A few rules hold regardless of how many guardians there are or who they are:

- **Guardianship is explicit and consensual.** A guardian has to sign to accept the role; nobody can be named a guardian without agreeing to it. Adding or removing a guardian is also a signed, auditable action, visible in the identity's history afterward.
- **A guardian can act on the ward's behalf for things the ward can't authorize alone.** Recovery is core to the method itself; a conformant registrar can also let a guardian act as the ward on an ongoing basis (see [token exchange](/docs/registrar/#10-delegation-chain-tokens-token-exchange), a registrar-profile capability, not something the method defines a dedicated operation for) -- similar to how a legal guardian already can act on behalf of a dependent, like a minor child.
- **A threshold decides how many guardians need to act together.** A ward can require any one guardian, a majority, all of them, or a specific count from 1 to 32, choosing the appropriate policy for the level of trust the situation calls for.
- **Each guardian action is signed with that specific guardian's key.** Whether a guardian is recovering a ward, authorizing something on its behalf, or removing another guardian, the action stays traceable to whichever guardian performed it, in the identity's history.
- **Guardianship is temporary by design.** It can be handed off, shared among several guardians, or re-established later, similar to how a legal guardianship relationship starts for a reason, and is expected to end at some point (e.g. when a minor child is no longer a minor). Removing the last guardian deactivates the identity by default; an identity whose policy opts into guardian-less operation ahead of time keeps going without one instead.

See the [formal specification](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/) for precise definitions of each operation and signature.


## Where it comes from


`did:guardian` combines two existing, proven DID methods, `did:plc` and `did:web`, and adds the guardianship concept on top of that.



**From [did:plc](https://github.com/did-method-plc/did-method-plc):** the *operation log*. An identity's history is an append-only, signed log of changes instead of a single mutable record. This is the same design Bluesky's `did:plc` runs for tens of millions of identities. This is also where *key rotation* comes from -- a guardian replaces a lost or compromised key by rotating forward to a new one.



**From [did:web](https://w3c-ccg.github.io/did-method-web/):** resolution by domain. For both `did:web` and `did:guardian`, there's no single central directory to query or depend on. An identity resolves through the domain that issued it. `did:guardian`'s identifier grammar deliberately mirrors `did:web`'s grammar (e.g. `did:guardian:acme.com:alice` vs `did:web:acme.com:alice`), so the two stay easy to read side by side.



**did:guardian's contribution:** group guardianship as a first-class part of the method. A configurable group of other identities can hold standing authority over a ward -- recovering it, acting on its behalf, with membership that can change hands over time -- verified the same way any other operation in the log is, with no separate credential, smart contract, or external system required. Neither `did:plc` nor `did:web` nor the W3C DID Core spec builds this in natively; `did:guardian` does.



**Compatibility.** Resolving a `did:guardian` identifier returns an ordinary [W3C DID Core](https://www.w3.org/TR/did-core/) document. Any tool that already understands DID documents understands this one. The guardian relationship lives in the method's operation log, which keeps the document shape fully ordinary.


## The identifier

```text {linenos=false}
did:guardian:acme.com:alice
did:guardian:acme.com
```




A `did:guardian` identifier is the domain that issued it, optionally followed by a name. `did:guardian:acme.com:alice` is Alice's identity at Acme's registrar. `did:guardian:acme.com` (no name at all) is Acme's own root organizational identity -- one per registrar, created the first time its registrar accepts any other identity.



Names are scoped to the registrar that issued them. The same name can exist, as two entirely unrelated identities, under two different domains, e.g. `did:guardian:acme.com:alice` and `did:guardian:fandom.com:alice` share nothing but a string. The full grammar, including the exact characters a name may contain, is in the [formal spec's §4](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#4-identifier).



## What you can do with it


**Sign in to an app with your Guardian ID.** The reference registrar also runs as a standard OpenID Connect provider. A third-party app's "sign in with your identity provider" option works against it same way that "Log in w/ Google" or Okta works. [guardianspec.org](https://guardianspec.org) is a running example: create an identity there, then use it to sign in anywhere that accepts a custom OIDC login.


**Set up a group-governed identity for a team or an AI agent.** A company can issue an identity for an agent it runs, name itself (or a specific set of people) as guardian, and set a threshold matching how much oversight the situation needs. The guardians can authorize actions the agent isn't allowed to approve on its own, recover it if its key is lost or compromised, or deactivate it once it's retired.


**Recover an identity after losing access to it.** A second key held in reserve, if there is one, can sign in a fresh key on its own. Otherwise, a group of the ward's own guardians (meeting the threshold its policy configures) can issue it one instead, without ever needing the lost key back. did:guardian uses guardianship for this case specifically, rather than only `did:plc`'s ordered recovery-key list -- and a guardian doesn't have to be a separate person: naming a cold-storage identity (a key generated once and kept offline) as its own guardian covers the same need with nobody else involved.


**Hand off responsibility cleanly.** Adding or removing a guardian is each its own signed operation, recorded permanently in the identity's history. Removing the last one deactivates the identity, unless its policy was set up ahead of time to keep it going guardian-less instead.

## The parts of this project


**The method.** The abstract rules, such as identifier syntax, the operation log, guardianship, signature requirements, which are independent of any specific server. Defined in the [formal specification](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/).



**The reference library** (`packages/lib`). A portable implementation of the method's cryptographic and verification logic, such as signing and verifying operations, replaying a log into current state, checking threshold rules. Implemented in TypeScript, using only Web Crypto, so it runs in Node, in a browser, or in serverless infrastructure like Cloudflare Workers.



**The reference registrar** (`packages/server`). A self-hostable server implementing the method, plus a working identity provider built on top of it: standard OpenID Connect (dynamic client registration, PKCE, refresh tokens, a full consent screen), an account dashboard, an admin console for an operator managing accounts on behalf of others, and an agent-identity API for a platform that creates and manages identities programmatically. All of this is documented separately in the [registrar API spec](/docs/registrar/). A custom registrar could implement only the method and remain fully conformant.



**The running reference deployment.** [guardianspec.org](https://guardianspec.org) is a live instance of the reference registrar. Consider running the registrar on your domain, and see how separate registrars operate independently -- names are scoped per domain, so nothing overlaps between them. Creating an identity is the fastest way to see the method work end to end.



## Learn more

- [**Get Started**](/docs/how-to/): a quickstart (create an identity, resolve it, add a guardian) plus task-oriented how-to guides -- give an AI agent a revocable identity, sign in via custom OIDC, self-host a registrar, recover after a lost key.
- [**Prior art and comparisons**](/docs/prior-art/): how did:guardian relates to did:webvh, KERI's delegated AIDs, the Sovrin Guardianship Task Force's work, and ERC-4337 social recovery -- and when each fits better.
- [**The formal specification**](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/): the normative, complete definition of the method. It contains each operation and signature rule, and the edge cases around them.
- [**The registrar API spec**](/docs/registrar/): everything the reference registrar adds beyond the method, including the OIDC provider, the account dashboard, the agent-identity API, etc.
- [**The GitHub repository**](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian): source for the method's reference library, the reference registrar, and this website.

# DID Guardian Method Specification, v0.2.0

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/

Status: Draft, 2026-11-22.

## 1. Overview

This section is non-normative.

A did:guardian identity is a signed, hash-chained log of operations, hosted at a domain. The identity's keys control it. Guardians are other did:guardian identities that the identity names, and each guardian records the identities it guards in its log. Guardians can recover the identity and govern it, under a policy the identity sets. The registrar for a domain hosts the logs for that domain, decides the order of their operations, and attests each new identity.

Every proof on an operation verifies from the log that contains it. When an operation involves another identity, the registrar checks that identity's current log before it accepts the operation. Resolvers check attestations and the state of guardian relationships.

did:guardian combines the hosting model of did:web, the signed log of did:plc, and guardianship.

## 2. Conformance

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 (RFC 2119, RFC 8174) when they appear in all capitals.

Sections 1, 12, 13 and Appendix A are non-normative. All other sections are normative.

This specification defines requirements for identities, registrars and resolvers.

## 3. Terminology

**identity**
: A DID of this method, and the log that defines it.

**operation**
: A JSON object that changes the state of an identity.

**log**
: The ordered list of all operations of an identity.

**state**
: The values that result from applying every operation of a log in order (Section 6).

**key**
: A P-256 public key.

**guardian**
: An identity named in another identity's `guardians`.

**ward**
: An identity that names a guardian.

**successor**
: An identity named in another identity's `successor`. It becomes the guardian when the last guardian is removed (Section 6.2).

**entry**
: The record of a guardian or a successor in a ward's state (REQ-6-2).

**registrar**
: The service that hosts the logs for a domain.

**root identity**
: The identity `did:guardian:<domain>`, which belongs to the registrar of that domain.

**operation hash**
: The hash of a complete operation (Section 5.2).

**version**
: The operation hash of an operation in a log. The version of a log is the operation hash of its last operation.

**anchor**
: The hash of parts of the first operation of a log (REQ-5-7).

## 4. Identifier

<a id="req-4-1"></a>**REQ-4-1.** A did:guardian DID MUST match one of these forms:

```
did:guardian:<domain>
did:guardian:<domain>:<name>
```

<a id="req-4-2"></a>**REQ-4-2.** `<domain>` MUST be a DNS hostname of two or more labels, in lowercase, at most 253 characters long. Each label MUST be 1 to 63 characters from `a`–`z`, `0`–`9` and `-`, and MUST begin and end with a letter or a digit. Internationalized names MUST use their A-label form. The last label MUST NOT consist only of digits.

<a id="req-4-3"></a>**REQ-4-3.** `<name>` MUST be 3 to 32 characters from `a`–`z`, `0`–`9` and `-`. It MUST begin and end with a letter or a digit.

<a id="req-4-4"></a>**REQ-4-4.** The form without `<name>` identifies the root identity of the domain.

<a id="req-4-5"></a>**REQ-4-5.** The path segment of an identity is its `<name>`, or `_` for the root identity.

<a id="req-4-6"></a>**REQ-4-6.** Two DIDs are equal if their strings are equal.

## 5. Encoding

### 5.1 Values

<a id="req-5-1"></a>**REQ-5-1.** An operation MUST be an I-JSON message (RFC 7493).

<a id="req-5-2"></a>**REQ-5-2.** Every number in an operation MUST have an integer value between 0 and 2^53 − 1.

<a id="req-5-3"></a>**REQ-5-3.** An operation MUST contain exactly the members that Section 7 defines for its type, and MAY also contain the members `extensions` and `critical` (Section 7.11). Every object inside an operation MUST contain exactly the members that this specification defines for it. A policy object MAY also contain the member `extensions`.

<a id="req-5-4"></a>**REQ-5-4.** The canonical form of a JSON value is its JSON Canonicalization Scheme serialization (RFC 8785).

<a id="req-5-5"></a>**REQ-5-5.** Two lists of keys are equal if they contain the same keys, in any order.

### 5.2 Hashes

<a id="req-5-6"></a>**REQ-5-6.** The hash of a JSON value is computed as follows:

1. Serialize the value in canonical form.
2. Compute the SHA-256 digest of the serialization.
3. Prefix the digest with the multihash header bytes `0x12 0x20`.
4. Encode the result as base58btc with the multibase prefix `z`.

The operation hash of an operation is the hash of the complete operation.

<a id="req-5-7"></a>**REQ-5-7.** The anchor of a log is the hash of its first operation with the `proof`, `attestation`, `guardians` and `successor` members removed.

### 5.3 Keys

<a id="req-5-8"></a>**REQ-5-8.** A key MUST be a P-256 public key encoded as a Multikey: the bytes `0x80 0x24` (the unsigned-varint encoding of multicodec `0x1200`), followed by the 33-byte compressed point, encoded as base58btc with the multibase prefix `z`.

<a id="req-5-9"></a>**REQ-5-9.** The compressed point MUST decode to a point on the P-256 curve.

### 5.4 Proofs

<a id="req-5-10"></a>**REQ-5-10.** An operation's `proof` member MUST be an array of Data Integrity proofs, sorted by `verificationMethod` in code-point order. Each proof secures the operation independently.

<a id="req-5-11"></a>**REQ-5-11.** Each proof MUST contain exactly these members:

| Member | Value |
|---|---|
| `type` | `"DataIntegrityProof"` |
| `cryptosuite` | `"ecdsa-jcs-2019"` |
| `verificationMethod` | `did:key:<key>#<key>` |
| `proofPurpose` | `"capabilityInvocation"` |
| `proofValue` | the signature |

<a id="req-5-12"></a>**REQ-5-12.** Proofs MUST be created and verified with the `ecdsa-jcs-2019` cryptosuite (W3C Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites v1.0), as follows:

1. The secured document is the operation with the `proof` and `attestation` members removed.
2. The proof configuration is the proof with the `proofValue` member removed.
3. The signed data is the SHA-256 digest of the canonical proof configuration, followed by the SHA-256 digest of the canonical secured document.
4. The signature is an ECDSA P-256 signature over the signed data, using SHA-256.
5. `proofValue` is the 64-byte signature value, R followed by S, encoded as base58btc with the multibase prefix `z`.

<a id="req-5-13"></a>**REQ-5-13.** The signature MUST use the low-S form. A verifier MUST reject a signature whose S value is greater than half the order of the P-256 curve.

<a id="req-5-14"></a>**REQ-5-14.** The signer of a proof is the key in its `verificationMethod`. A proof is valid if its signature verifies with that key.

<a id="req-5-15"></a>**REQ-5-15.** An operation MUST NOT contain two proofs from the same key.

<a id="req-5-16"></a>**REQ-5-16.** A key approves an operation if the operation contains a valid proof from that key. A guardian or successor approves an operation if at least one key in its entry approves it.

## 6. State

<a id="req-6-1"></a>**REQ-6-1.** The state of an identity consists of:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `keys` | a list of 1 to 8 distinct keys |
| `guardians` | a list of 0 to 32 entries with distinct DIDs |
| `successor` | an entry, or `null` |
| `wards` | a list of ward records with distinct DIDs |
| `policy` | a policy object (Section 6.3) |
| `services` | a list of 0 to 32 services with distinct `id` values |
| `alsoKnownAs` | a list of 0 to 32 distinct URIs (RFC 3986) |
| `deactivated` | `true` or `false` |
| `critical` | a list of distinct extension names (Section 7.11) |

<a id="req-6-2"></a>**REQ-6-2.** An entry MUST contain exactly the members `did`, `anchor`, `keys` and `consent`. `did` is a did:guardian DID. `anchor` is the anchor of that DID's log. `keys` is a list of 1 to 8 distinct keys. `consent` is the operation hash of an `acceptWard` in that DID's log.

<a id="req-6-3"></a>**REQ-6-3.** A key MUST NOT appear more than once across `keys`, the `keys` of every entry in `guardians`, and the `keys` of `successor`.

<a id="req-6-4"></a>**REQ-6-4.** A ward record MUST contain exactly the members `did` and `anchor`. `did` is a did:guardian DID. `anchor` is the anchor of that DID's log.

<a id="req-6-5"></a>**REQ-6-5.** The DID of an identity MUST NOT appear in its `guardians`, its `successor` or its `wards`. The DID of `successor` MUST NOT appear in `guardians`.

<a id="req-6-6"></a>**REQ-6-6.** A service MUST contain exactly the members `id`, `type` and `serviceEndpoint`. `id` MUST be `#` followed by a DID URL fragment. `type` MUST be a string. `serviceEndpoint` MUST be a URI (RFC 3986).

<a id="req-6-7"></a>**REQ-6-7.** After each operation, the state MUST conform to REQ-6-1 through REQ-6-6 and Section 6.3.

### 6.1 Required approvals

<a id="req-6-8"></a>**REQ-6-8.** Let N be the number of guardians in the state before an operation. Let E be the number of guardians eligible to approve it. E equals N − 1 for `removeGuardian`, and N for every other operation. For a setting value v, the number of guardian approvals required is computed as follows:

1. Start with a base value: 1 for `"any"`, floor(E / 2) + 1 for `"majority"`, E for `"all"`, and the smaller of k and E for an integer k.
2. If v is not `"any"` and N is at least 2, raise the value to at least 2.
3. For `membership` and for the `threshold` of `deactivation`, raise the value to at least floor(N / 2) + 1.

<a id="req-6-9"></a>**REQ-6-9.** A clause of REQ-7-6 that requires guardians per a setting cannot be met if E is 0 or if the required number is greater than E.

### 6.2 Orphaning

<a id="req-6-10"></a>**REQ-6-10.** When a `removeGuardian` leaves `guardians` empty, the state changes according to `policy.orphan`:

| `orphan` | Change |
|---|---|
| `"deactivate"` | `deactivated` becomes `true` |
| `"independent"` | no change |
| `"successor"` | the `successor` entry becomes the only entry in `guardians`, `successor` becomes `null`, and `orphan` becomes `"deactivate"` |

### 6.3 Policy

<a id="req-6-11"></a>**REQ-6-11.** A policy object MAY contain these members. A member that is absent takes its default value.

| Member | Governs | Allowed values | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `recovery` | guardian approval of `update`, `acceptWard` and `releaseWard` | `"any"`, `"majority"`, `"all"`, integer k | `"majority"` |
| `membership` | guardian approval of `addGuardian` and `setPolicy` | `"majority"`, `"all"`, integer k | `"majority"` |
| `removal` | guardian approval of `removeGuardian` | `"any"`, `"majority"`, `"all"`, integer k | `"majority"` |
| `deactivation` | approval of `deactivate` | a deactivation object (REQ-6-12) | `{"by": "both", "threshold": "majority"}` |
| `orphan` | the change when the last guardian is removed (REQ-6-10) | `"deactivate"`, `"independent"`, `"successor"` | `"deactivate"` |
| `maxWards` | the largest allowed size of `wards` | integer k ≥ 1 | no limit |

<a id="req-6-12"></a>**REQ-6-12.** A deactivation object MUST contain exactly the members `by` and `threshold`. `by` MUST be one of `"self"`, `"guardians"`, `"either"` or `"both"`. `threshold` MUST be `"majority"`, `"all"` or an integer k.

<a id="req-6-13"></a>**REQ-6-13.** An integer k in `recovery`, `membership`, `removal` or `threshold` MUST be between 1 and 32.

<a id="req-6-14"></a>**REQ-6-14.** `orphan` MUST be `"successor"` if `successor` is an entry, and MUST NOT be `"successor"` if `successor` is `null`.

<a id="req-6-15"></a>**REQ-6-15.** If `maxWards` is present, `wards` MUST NOT contain more than `maxWards` records.

## 7. Operations

### 7.1 Common members

<a id="req-7-1"></a>**REQ-7-1.** Every operation MUST contain the members `type`, `prev` and `proof`.

<a id="req-7-2"></a>**REQ-7-2.** `type` MUST be one of `create`, `update`, `addGuardian`, `updateGuardian`, `removeGuardian`, `setPolicy`, `acceptWard`, `releaseWard` or `deactivate`.

<a id="req-7-3"></a>**REQ-7-3.** The first operation of a log MUST be a `create`. A later operation MUST NOT be a `create`.

<a id="req-7-4"></a>**REQ-7-4.** In a `create`, `prev` MUST be `null`. In every other operation, `prev` MUST be the operation hash of the preceding operation.

### 7.2 Approval rules

In the following rules:
- "one current key" means approval by at least one key in `keys` in the state before the operation;
- "guardians per s" means approvals from the number of current guardians that REQ-6-8 requires for setting s;
- "every key in X" means approval by every key in the list X in the operation.

For a `create`, the state before the operation is empty and N is 0.

<a id="req-7-5"></a>**REQ-7-5.** Every proof on an operation MUST come from one of these keys: a key in `keys`, in an entry in `guardians`, or in `successor`, in the state before the operation; or a key in a list of keys in the operation.

<a id="req-7-6"></a>**REQ-7-6.** An operation MUST have the approvals that the following table requires.

| Type | Required approvals |
|---|---|
| `create` | every key in `keys`; every key in each entry in `guardians`; every key in `successor`, if it is an entry |
| `update` | every key in `keys`; and either one current key or guardians per `recovery` |
| `addGuardian` | every key in `entry`; one current key; and guardians per `membership`, if N > 0 |
| `updateGuardian` | every key in `keys`; and either a key in the named entry, or one current key together with one guardian other than the named one |
| `removeGuardian` | one of: the removed guardian, if N ≥ 2; guardians per `removal`, from the guardians other than the removed one; one current key, if `evidence` is present; or one current key together with the successor, if N = 1 and `successor` is an entry |
| `setPolicy` | one current key; guardians per `membership`, if N > 0; and every key in `successor`, if it is an entry that differs from the current `successor` |
| `acceptWard` | one current key, or guardians per `recovery` |
| `releaseWard` | one current key, or guardians per `recovery` |
| `deactivate` | if N = 0, one current key; otherwise, as `policy.deactivation.by` specifies: `self`, one current key; `guardians`, guardians per `deactivation.threshold`; `either`, one of the two; `both`, both |

### 7.3 create

<a id="req-7-7"></a>**REQ-7-7.** A `create` MUST contain the members `type`, `did`, `keys`, `guardians`, `successor`, `policy`, `services`, `alsoKnownAs`, `prev` and `proof`. The `create` of an identity other than a root identity MUST contain the member `attestation`. The `create` of a root identity MUST NOT contain it.

<a id="req-7-8"></a>**REQ-7-8.** `did` is the DID of the identity. `keys`, `guardians`, `successor`, `policy`, `services` and `alsoKnownAs` set the initial state. `wards` is empty and `deactivated` is `false`.

<a id="req-7-9"></a>**REQ-7-9.** `attestation` MUST be a Data Integrity proof as in REQ-5-11, except that its `cryptosuite` may be any string and its `verificationMethod` is `did:guardian:<domain>?versionId=<version>#key-<n>`, where `<domain>` is the domain of `did`, `<version>` is a version of the root identity's log, and `<n>` is a decimal integer without leading zeros. It secures the same document as the other proofs (REQ-5-12). Section 11 defines how it is verified.

### 7.4 update

<a id="req-7-10"></a>**REQ-7-10.** An `update` MUST contain the members `type`, `keys`, `services`, `alsoKnownAs`, `prev` and `proof`.

<a id="req-7-11"></a>**REQ-7-11.** `update` replaces `keys`, `services` and `alsoKnownAs` in the state.

### 7.5 addGuardian

<a id="req-7-12"></a>**REQ-7-12.** An `addGuardian` MUST contain the members `type`, `entry`, `prev` and `proof`. `entry` is an entry (REQ-6-2).

<a id="req-7-13"></a>**REQ-7-13.** The DID of `entry` MUST NOT already be a guardian.

<a id="req-7-14"></a>**REQ-7-14.** `addGuardian` appends `entry` to `guardians`.

### 7.6 updateGuardian

<a id="req-7-15"></a>**REQ-7-15.** An `updateGuardian` MUST contain the members `type`, `guardian`, `keys`, `prev` and `proof`. `guardian` is the DID of a current guardian or of the successor.

<a id="req-7-16"></a>**REQ-7-16.** `updateGuardian` replaces the `keys` of the entry for `guardian`.

### 7.7 removeGuardian

<a id="req-7-17"></a>**REQ-7-17.** A `removeGuardian` MUST contain the members `type`, `guardian`, `prev` and `proof`. It MAY contain the member `evidence`. `guardian` is the DID of a current guardian.

<a id="req-7-18"></a>**REQ-7-18.** If present, `evidence` is the operation hash of a `deactivate`, or of a `releaseWard` whose `ward` is this identity, in the log of `guardian`.

<a id="req-7-19"></a>**REQ-7-19.** `removeGuardian` removes the entry for `guardian`, and then applies REQ-6-10.

### 7.8 setPolicy

<a id="req-7-20"></a>**REQ-7-20.** A `setPolicy` MUST contain the members `type`, `policy`, `successor`, `prev` and `proof`. `successor` is an entry or `null`.

<a id="req-7-21"></a>**REQ-7-21.** `setPolicy` replaces `policy` and `successor` in the state.

### 7.9 acceptWard and releaseWard

<a id="req-7-22"></a>**REQ-7-22.** A `acceptWard` MUST contain the members `type`, `ward`, `prev` and `proof`. `ward` is a ward record (REQ-6-4).

<a id="req-7-23"></a>**REQ-7-23.** The DID of `ward` MUST NOT already be in `wards`.

<a id="req-7-24"></a>**REQ-7-24.** `acceptWard` appends `ward` to `wards`. It records that the identity consents to be a guardian or successor of that ward.

<a id="req-7-25"></a>**REQ-7-25.** An `releaseWard` MUST contain the members `type`, `ward`, `prev` and `proof`. `ward` is the DID of a record in `wards`.

<a id="req-7-26"></a>**REQ-7-26.** `releaseWard` removes the record for `ward` from `wards`. It records that the identity withdraws its consent.

### 7.10 deactivate

<a id="req-7-27"></a>**REQ-7-27.** A `deactivate` MUST contain the members `type`, `prev` and `proof`.

<a id="req-7-28"></a>**REQ-7-28.** `deactivate` sets `deactivated` to `true`.

### 7.11 Extensions

<a id="req-7-29"></a>**REQ-7-29.** `extensions` is an object. Each member name is an extension name, and each value is defined by that extension. An extension name MUST be an absolute URI.

<a id="req-7-30"></a>**REQ-7-30.** `critical` is a non-empty list of distinct extension names. Only a `create` or a `setPolicy` MAY contain `critical`. Each name in `critical` MUST be a member of the `extensions` of the operation's `policy`. The configuration of a critical extension is held only in `policy.extensions`.

<a id="req-7-31"></a>**REQ-7-31.** An extension affects whether an operation is valid only while its name is in the state's `critical`.

<a id="req-7-32"></a>**REQ-7-32.** An operation adds each name in its `critical` to the state's `critical`, if it is not already there. A name in the state's `critical` remains there for every later operation of the log.

<a id="req-7-33"></a>**REQ-7-33.** An extension MAY add requirements to operations. An extension MUST NOT remove or weaken a requirement of this specification.

<a id="req-7-34"></a>**REQ-7-34.** A verifier MUST ignore every extension whose name is not in the state's `critical`, whether or not it implements that extension. Ignored extensions remain part of the operation hash and the secured document. The contents of an extension value are defined by the extension, not by REQ-5-3.

<a id="req-7-35"></a>**REQ-7-35.** An extension defines how its configuration changes. A change to an extension's configuration requires the approvals that this specification requires for the operation that makes it.

## 8. Verification

<a id="req-8-1"></a>**REQ-8-1.** A verifier MUST verify the log of a DID by the following steps, and report one of three results. An operation is **unsupported** if the state's `critical` before it, or the operation's `critical`, names an extension that the verifier does not implement, or if its `type`, or the `cryptosuite` of one of its proofs, has a value that the verifier does not implement. The verifier processes operations in order and stops at the first operation that is unsupported or that fails a step. Within one operation, the unsupported conditions are checked before the steps. It reports **unsupported** or **invalid** for that operation, or **valid** if no operation stops it. A verifier MUST NOT treat an unsupported log as valid.

1. The log is a non-empty array of operations.
2. The first operation is a `create` whose `did` equals the DID.
3. Each later operation's `prev` equals the operation hash of the operation before it.
4. No operation follows a state in which `deactivated` is `true`.
5. For each operation in order:
   1. The operation conforms to Sections 5 and 7.
   2. Every proof is valid (REQ-5-14) and comes from a permitted key (REQ-7-5).
   3. The approvals meet the rule in REQ-7-6, evaluated against the state before the operation.
   4. Apply the operation to the state, and check that the result conforms to Section 6.

<a id="req-8-2"></a>**REQ-8-2.** Verification of a log depends only on that log. It does not depend on other logs or on the time of verification.

## 9. DID document

<a id="req-9-1"></a>**REQ-9-1.** The DID document of an identity is derived from its state after the last operation of its log.

<a id="req-9-2"></a>**REQ-9-2.** If the state is not deactivated, the DID document MUST contain exactly:

| Member | Value |
|---|---|
| `@context` | `["https://www.w3.org/ns/did/v1", "https://w3id.org/security/multikey/v1"]` |
| `id` | the DID |
| `verificationMethod` | for each key at index n of `keys`: `{"id": "<did>#key-<n>", "type": "Multikey", "controller": "<did>", "publicKeyMultibase": "<key>"}` |
| `authentication`, `assertionMethod`, `capabilityInvocation` | the `id` of every verification method |
| `service` | the services, each with its `id` prefixed by the DID; an empty list if there are none |
| `alsoKnownAs` | the `alsoKnownAs` list, if it is not empty |

<a id="req-9-3"></a>**REQ-9-3.** If the state is deactivated, the DID document MUST contain exactly `@context` and `id`.

<a id="req-9-4"></a>**REQ-9-4.** DID document metadata MUST include `versionId`, the version of the log, and `anchor`, the anchor of the log. If the state is deactivated, DID document metadata MUST include `"deactivated": true`.

<a id="req-9-5"></a>**REQ-9-5.** Resolving a DID URL with the parameter `versionId=<version>` yields the DID document derived from the state after the operation whose operation hash is `<version>`. Only the log up to and including that operation needs to verify.

## 10. Registrar

### 10.1 Resources

<a id="req-10-1"></a>**REQ-10-1.** The registrar for a domain MUST serve these resources over HTTPS at `https://<domain>/.well-known/guardian/<segment>`, where `<segment>` is the path segment of the identity (REQ-4-5):

| Method and path | Response |
|---|---|
| `GET .../<segment>/log` | the log, as a JSON array in log order |
| `GET .../<segment>` | the DID document |
| `POST .../<segment>/operations` | accepts one operation as the request body |

<a id="req-10-2"></a>**REQ-10-2.** A `GET` request MUST NOT change any state.

<a id="req-10-3"></a>**REQ-10-3.** A registrar MUST NOT serve two logs for one DID where neither is a prefix of the other.

<a id="req-10-4"></a>**REQ-10-4.** A registrar MUST respond to a rejected operation with HTTP status 400 and a JSON object with an `error` member that describes the reason.

### 10.2 Accepting operations

<a id="req-10-5"></a>**REQ-10-5.** A registrar MUST accept an operation only if all of these hold:

1. Its `prev` equals the version of the log, or it is a `create` for a path segment that has no log.
2. The log, with the operation appended, is valid (Section 8). An unsupported result is a rejection.
3. Every check in REQ-10-7 that applies to the operation holds.

<a id="req-10-6"></a>**REQ-10-6.** An entry has standing for an identity if the current log of the entry's `did` verifies and, in that log:

1. the anchor equals the entry's `anchor`;
2. the state is not deactivated;
3. the state's `keys` equal the entry's `keys`;
4. `consent` is an `acceptWard` whose `ward` names the identity's DID and anchor;
5. the state's `wards` contains that record.

<a id="req-10-7"></a>**REQ-10-7.** Before accepting an operation, a registrar MUST fetch the current log of each other identity that the operation involves, and check:

| Case | Check |
|---|---|
| an operation adds or replaces an entry | the new entry has standing |
| a guardian or successor approves an operation | its entry has standing, except for item 3 when the operation is an `updateGuardian` for that guardian or successor |
| an `updateGuardian` | the new `keys` equal the `keys` in the current state of `guardian` |
| a `removeGuardian` with `evidence` | in the log of `guardian`, the anchor equals the entry's `anchor`; `evidence` is a `deactivate`, or a `releaseWard` whose `ward` is this identity, and it follows the entry's `consent`; and the entry does not have standing because of item 2 or item 5 of REQ-10-6 |
| a `removeGuardian` that promotes the successor (REQ-6-10) | the successor's entry has standing |
| an `acceptWard` | if the ward's DID has a log, the `ward` record names its anchor |

<a id="req-10-8"></a>**REQ-10-8.** A registrar MUST accept at most one operation for each value of `prev`.

<a id="req-10-9"></a>**REQ-10-9.** For a `create`, the registrar MUST also require that the DID's domain is its domain and that the name is unused (REQ-10-12). It MUST add the `attestation`, using a key of its root identity and the current version of the root identity's log, before it applies REQ-10-5.

<a id="req-10-10"></a>**REQ-10-10.** A registrar MUST create its root identity before it accepts any other `create`.

<a id="req-10-11"></a>**REQ-10-11.** A registrar MUST NOT remove or alter an accepted operation. A registrar MUST continue to serve the log of a deactivated identity.

<a id="req-10-12"></a>**REQ-10-12.** A name, once used, MUST NOT be used for another identity.

### 10.3 Held keys

<a id="req-10-13"></a>**REQ-10-13.** A registrar that holds a private key for an identity MUST create a proof with that key only in response to a request authenticated as that identity.

<a id="req-10-14"></a>**REQ-10-14.** Apart from the `attestation`, one request MUST NOT cause a registrar to create proofs for more than one identity.

## 11. Resolution

<a id="req-11-1"></a>**REQ-11-1.** To resolve a DID, a resolver MUST:

1. fetch the log from the registrar of the DID's domain;
2. verify the log (Section 8);
3. verify the `attestation` of its `create`, unless the DID is a root identity (REQ-11-2);
4. derive the DID document (Section 9).

<a id="req-11-2"></a>**REQ-11-2.** A resolver that does not implement the `cryptosuite` of an `attestation` MUST report the attestation as unsupported. Otherwise, an `attestation` is valid if the log of the root identity of the DID's domain contains the operation named by `versionId`, that log up to and including that operation verifies, the state after that operation is not deactivated and has a key at index `<n>`, and the signature verifies with that key.

<a id="req-11-3"></a>**REQ-11-3.** A resolver SHOULD record the anchor and the version of each log it fetches.

<a id="req-11-4"></a>**REQ-11-4.** If a later fetch of a log yields a different anchor, the resolver MUST report that the DID refers to a different identity. If it yields a log that does not contain the recorded version, the resolver MUST report that the log was rolled back or forked.

<a id="req-11-5"></a>**REQ-11-5.** For each entry in `guardians` and `successor`, a resolver MAY fetch the log of the entry's `did` and report the first result in this table whose condition holds:

| Result | Condition |
|---|---|
| unavailable | the log cannot be fetched or does not verify |
| different identity | the log's anchor differs from the entry's `anchor` |
| deactivated | the state is deactivated |
| withdrawn | `consent` is not an `acceptWard` that names this identity's DID and anchor, or `wards` does not contain that record |
| keys out of date | the state's `keys` differ from the entry's `keys` |
| mutual | none of the above |

<a id="req-11-6"></a>**REQ-11-6.** For each record in `wards`, a resolver MAY fetch the log of the record's `did` and report the first result whose condition holds: unavailable, if the log cannot be fetched or does not verify; different identity, if its anchor differs from the record's `anchor`; guardian, if its `guardians` has an entry for this identity; successor, if its `successor` is an entry for this identity; otherwise, not related.

<a id="req-11-7"></a>**REQ-11-7.** A resolver MUST NOT present a guardianship as mutual unless REQ-11-5 reports mutual or keys out of date.

<a id="req-11-8"></a>**REQ-11-8.** A resolver MAY verify a log that another party presents. A presented log is current only as of its version.

## 12. Security considerations

This section is non-normative.

**Order of operations.** Every proof is verifiable from its log, but the registrar decides the order in which operations are accepted. A verifier relies on the registrar for that order, as with did:web and did:plc.

**Checks at acceptance.** The checks in REQ-10-7 compare an operation with other logs at the time of acceptance. A verifier does not repeat them. A resolver can compare current logs (REQ-11-5), but cannot tell what another log contained at the time of acceptance. Removal with `evidence` depends on these checks; it also requires one current key, so a registrar alone cannot use it.

**Joining and leaving.** A guardian records `acceptWard` before the ward adds it, because REQ-10-7 requires the consent to exist. A guardian that leaves SHOULD remove itself from the ward before it records `releaseWard`. A guardian that records `releaseWard` first, or that deactivates, loses standing, so a registrar rejects its approvals for that ward (REQ-10-7), and the ward can remove it with `evidence`. Evidence counts only if it follows the guardian's current consent, so a `releaseWard` from an earlier period of guardianship cannot be reused.

**Guardian keys.** A ward's entry holds a copy of the guardian's keys. When a guardian replaces its keys, it updates each of its entries with `updateGuardian`; its `wards` lists them. Until then, a registrar rejects approvals made with the old keys (REQ-10-7). A successor's entry is updated with `updateGuardian` or `setPolicy`. A resolver reports entries whose keys are out of date (REQ-11-5).

**Stolen guardian key.** A party that holds a guardian's current key can act as that guardian in every ward until each ward removes the entry or the guardian replaces its keys.

**Lost guardian key.** A guardian that loses its key recovers its identity through its guardians. Each ward then updates the entry with one current key and one other guardian (REQ-7-6). A ward whose only guardian lost its key cannot update the entry; its successor, if any, can replace that guardian.

**Sole guardian.** A sole guardian that leaves SHOULD first approve the addition of a replacement, then remove itself. A sole guardian that dies or withdraws without a replacement cannot be replaced by the ward's keys alone, because the ward cannot add a guardian, name a successor or change `orphan` without its guardians. The ward can then only remove the guardian with `evidence`, which applies `orphan`. A successor refreshes its entry with `updateGuardian`.

**Mutual guardians.** If two identities are each other's only guardian, one stolen key gives control of both: the holder replaces the keys of one identity, then uses it as guardian to replace the keys of the other. Give each identity at least one guardian outside such a pair.

**Stolen key.** A party that holds a stolen key can act as the identity until the guardians replace the key. Those operations remain in the log.

**Unilateral settings.** `recovery: "any"` lets one guardian replace the keys. `removal: "any"` lets one guardian remove another; with two guardians, either can remove the other. `deactivation.by: "self"` or `"either"` lets anyone who holds a key end the identity. Choose these settings deliberately.

**Two guardians.** With two guardians and `removal` other than `"any"`, neither guardian can remove the other. Use three or more guardians, or set `removal: "any"`.

**Orphaning.** Every way to remove the last guardian requires one current key. Under the default `orphan: "deactivate"`, the identity is then deactivated, and deactivation is permanent. To lower the risk, use guardians on more than one domain, or name a successor.

**Unavailable guardians.** A registrar cannot check the standing of a guardian whose log cannot be fetched, so it cannot accept that guardian's approvals or changes to its entry, or a removal with `evidence`. If no guardian can approve, operations that need guardians cannot be accepted. A successor can act only when there is one guardian.

**Successor.** A successor and one current key can replace a sole guardian, and the successor then becomes the guardian. Name only a successor you trust with that power.

**One-sided records.** Any identity can record `acceptWard` for any ward. A guardianship is mutual only when REQ-11-5 reports it.

**Unsupported operations.** A registrar, or a party that presents a log, can append an operation with an unknown `type` or `cryptosuite`. A verifier then reports the log as unsupported. This has the same effect as withholding the log, and resolvers detect it by the recorded version (REQ-11-4).

**Forks.** Any party that holds the keys can sign two different operations with the same `prev`. Any party can also remove an unneeded proof from an operation, which produces a different operation hash. A registrar accepts only one operation for each `prev` (REQ-10-8). Resolvers detect a fork by the recorded version (REQ-11-4).

**Anchor.** The anchor does not cover the initial `guardians` and `successor`. Two `create` operations that differ only in those members have the same anchor; a registrar accepts one of them.

**Extensions.** A verifier that does not implement a critical extension reports the log as unsupported, never valid. An extension that is not listed in `critical` has no effect on validity for any verifier, so an extension that changes who may approve an operation must be made critical. Only `create` and `setPolicy` can make an extension critical, so adding one requires the same approvals as a policy change. A critical extension cannot be removed from a log, so every later verifier must implement it.

**Hostile registrar.** A registrar cannot forge proofs. It can refuse operations, serve an outdated or forged log to a resolver that has not seen the identity before, or skip the checks in REQ-10-7. Resolvers detect a replaced, rolled-back or forked log by its anchor and recorded version (REQ-11-4). A registrar that serves a forged log for a guardian on its domain can mislead a ward that adds that guardian; the ward detects this if it knows the guardian's anchor. A registrar that skips the checks in REQ-10-7 lets a party with one current key remove guardians with false `evidence`, and lets retired or withdrawn guardian keys approve operations.

**Root identity.** The root identity's key attests every `create` on its domain. A party with that key, or with an old root key, can attest a forged `create` for an unused name. Recorded anchors protect identities that a resolver has seen before.

**Domain transfer.** A new owner of a domain controls its registrar. The new owner cannot produce logs that match recorded anchors.

**Registrar-held keys.** A registrar that holds an identity's key can create proofs as that identity. REQ-10-13 and REQ-10-14 limit when it may do so, but no other party can check that limit.

**Checking a registrar.** Registrar requirements fall into three groups:

| Group | Who can check | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| Provable from logs | anyone, by fetching and verifying logs | REQ-10-5 (items 1 and 2), REQ-10-11, REQ-10-12 |
| Testable | an operator, against a test deployment | REQ-10-1, REQ-10-2, REQ-10-4, REQ-10-8, REQ-10-9, REQ-10-10 |
| Trusted | no other party | REQ-10-3, REQ-10-7, REQ-10-13, REQ-10-14 |

## 13. Privacy considerations

This section is non-normative.

Logs are public and permanent. Every key, guardian relationship, ward, policy, service and alias that an identity has ever had is visible to anyone. A guardian's `wards` lists every identity it guards. Do not put personal data in names, services or `alsoKnownAs`.

## Appendix A. Examples

This appendix is non-normative. Hashes, keys and signatures are shortened with `…`, and proofs are abbreviated to their `verificationMethod`.

Bob agrees to guard Alice. Alice's client computes the anchor of her `create`, which does not depend on her guardians (REQ-5-7). Bob records `acceptWard` in his log:

```json
{
  "type": "acceptWard",
  "ward": {"did": "did:guardian:acme.com:alice", "anchor": "zQmAliceAnchor…"},
  "prev": "zQmBob1…",
  "proof": [{"verificationMethod": "did:key:zDnaeBob…#zDnaeBob…", "…": "…"}]
}
```

Bob's `acceptWard` has operation hash `zQmBobAccept…`. Alice's `create` names Bob as a guardian:

```json
{
  "type": "create",
  "did": "did:guardian:acme.com:alice",
  "keys": ["zDnaeAlice…"],
  "guardians": [
    {
      "did": "did:guardian:acme.com:bob",
      "anchor": "zQmBobAnchor…",
      "keys": ["zDnaeBob…"],
      "consent": "zQmBobAccept…"
    }
  ],
  "successor": null,
  "policy": {},
  "services": [],
  "alsoKnownAs": [],
  "prev": null,
  "proof": [
    {"verificationMethod": "did:key:zDnaeAlice…#zDnaeAlice…", "…": "…"},
    {"verificationMethod": "did:key:zDnaeBob…#zDnaeBob…", "…": "…"}
  ],
  "attestation": {"verificationMethod": "did:guardian:acme.com?versionId=zQmRoot…#key-0", "…": "…"}
}
```

Bob replaces the key in his log, then updates his entry in Alice's log. In this example, `zDnaeBob…` sorts before `zDnaeBobNew…`; real keys sort by their full encoded values (REQ-5-10):

```json
{
  "type": "updateGuardian",
  "guardian": "did:guardian:acme.com:bob",
  "keys": ["zDnaeBobNew…"],
  "prev": "zQmAliceCreate…",
  "proof": [
    {"verificationMethod": "did:key:zDnaeBob…#zDnaeBob…", "…": "…"},
    {"verificationMethod": "did:key:zDnaeBobNew…#zDnaeBobNew…", "…": "…"}
  ]
}
```

Required guardian approvals under the default policy:

| Guardians (N) | `recovery` | `membership` | `removal` | `deactivation` (guardian part) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | not possible | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | not possible | 2 |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 5 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 |

A sole guardian is removed with `evidence` and one current key, or by the successor and one current key. `orphan` then applies.

## Changelog

This draft replaces all earlier drafts of v0.2.0. Earlier drafts are in the repository history.

- **2026-11-22**: REQ-5-2 constrains the value of a number, not its written form.


---

# did:guardian Registrar API, v1 (the reference registrar)

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/registrar/

**Version 1.** This document is a registrar profile, not the method: exactly one registrar implementation's HTTP surface -- `packages/server` in this repository, deployed as guardianspec.org's registrar. It is versioned and evolves independently of [the formal method specification](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/) -- adding, removing, or reshaping anything here never changes method conformance, and a different registrar implementation is free to expose none of it. Only [§1](#1-method-required-endpoints) restates an actual method requirement (§10 of the formal spec); everything else is this registrar's operational choice.

Most endpoints below are rooted at `/.well-known/guardian/<name>` (or `/.well-known/guardian/_` for the bare-domain identity) -- §1 through §4 and §13. Registration, login, OIDC, the account dashboard, the admin console, and the pending-operation browser page live at their own top-level paths instead (§2, §5, §8, §9, §14, and `/.well-known/guardian/pending/<id>`, not name-scoped). All request/response bodies are JSON unless noted.

## 1. Method-required endpoints

Required by the formal spec's [REQ-10-1](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-1); this registrar's implementation of them.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/.well-known/guardian/<name>` | current derived DID Document |
| `GET` | `/.well-known/guardian/<name>/log` | full operation log, in order |
| `POST` | `/.well-known/guardian/<name>/operations` | submit one fully-proofed operation |

Both `GET` endpoints are plain reads -- neither one ever creates anything, including the bare-domain root identity itself ([REQ-10-2](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-2)).

`POST .../operations` accepts any operation type from the formal spec's §7 with every required proof already attached and appends it if valid, rejecting with a reason string otherwise. This is the only path by which an *externally* pre-proofed operation (e.g. two guardians who coordinated their own signatures out-of-band) reaches the log directly, without going through §3's collection machinery. On success, the response is `{accepted: true, operation}` -- the accepted operation, with its attestation attached if it's a `create`; on rejection, `{error: <reason>}` with HTTP 400 ([REQ-10-4](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-4)). A `create` submitted here for a named identity gets exactly `/register`'s gate (§2): no session or bearer token can exist yet for a DID that doesn't exist yet, so it's anonymous self-service -- rate-limited to 5 attempts per 10 minutes per client IP (HTTP 429 past that), and rejected outright with HTTP 403 when this deployment has closed public registration (`REGISTRATION_MODE`, below). Every other operation type is ungated here beyond its approval requirement -- the proofs already attached are the authorization.

## 2. Self-contained convenience endpoints

`/register` and `.../adopt` also live at this level, but this page doesn't yet describe their own mechanics in detail -- a change to how registration names an initial guardian is under discussion. §9 has what's settled.

Each of these corresponds to an operation whose own required approvals a single call from one authenticated party can satisfy, with this registrar producing every proof it needs to from keys it already holds -- no new authority is ever granted to a third party by any of these. `.../remove` is the one row here whose safety isn't just "no new authority granted": it also depends on the acceptance-time check (REQ-10-7) actually verifying the caller's claimed evidence names a genuine `deactivate` or `releaseWard`, not merely trusting that it does -- a caller can name any evidence hash it wants, and a bogus one is rejected there, not here. Auth model for all of them: either an active `gw_session` cookie, or a trusted OIDC client credential (Basic auth) acting on an already-verified decision made by its caller -- always for *whichever identity this operation actually needs a proof from*, never assumed from the identity named in the path. `.../remove-self` in particular authenticates the departing guardian, not the ward in the URL -- a held key signs only on a request already authenticated as that exact identity ([REQ-10-13](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-13)).

**What makes an OIDC client "trusted."** `client_id`/`client_secret` (Basic auth) alone is never enough -- a client row also carries its `trusted` flag, checked explicitly. Every client created through `POST /oauth/register-client` (RFC 7591's open, unauthenticated dynamic registration) starts `trusted = false`, with no field in that request able to change it; there is no endpoint, anywhere on this registrar, that sets it to `true`. The only way a client becomes trusted is a direct operator database write -- an out-of-band, deployment-level decision this registrar's HTTP surface has no way to grant itself. This is why dynamic client registration staying unauthenticated is safe at all: a self-registered client can authenticate its OIDC flows, but gets nothing from this section's endpoints regardless of what credentials it presents.

| Method | Path | Operation produced | Why it's self-contained |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `.../rotate` | `update`, both approvals self-produced | this registrar holds both the identity's current key and the fresh one it just generated, so it signs with both itself |
| `POST` | `.../take-custody` | `update` to a caller-supplied key | the caller's proof of possession for the new key, combined with this registrar's proof using the key it's about to stop holding |
| `POST` | `.../remove-self` | `removeGuardian`, the departing guardian itself | needs only the departing guardian's approval -- the "removed guardian itself, if there are at least two" path |
| `POST` | `.../remove` | `removeGuardian`, with evidence | the *ward's own* key, naming evidence (a `deactivate` or `releaseWard` already in the departing guardian's log) that the guardian already lost standing |

A forced removal by vote of the *other* guardians, with no evidence, or a deactivation needing guardian cooperation too, needs more than this registrar can produce from one call -- see §3.

**`.../take-custody` is irreversible in a way nothing else on this page is.** Every other row above produces an operation and nothing changes about who's custodied going forward. This one ends it: body `{operation, proof}`, where `operation` is an `update` naming the caller's new key (with its current `services`/`alsoKnownAs` carried over) and `proof` is that same key's [Data Integrity proof](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-5-11) of possession, built by the caller before this call. This registrar can never produce that proof itself, since it will never hold the new key's private half. A stale `prev` by the time the request arrives just fails the way any other `prev` mismatch does. Afterward, this registrar has deleted its held key for that identity outright -- not set it aside, not kept it for a future rotation, gone. Every row on this page that needs a held key stops working for that identity from then on, with a clear error pointing at submitting pre-proofed operations through §1 directly instead.

Nothing here stops the bare-domain root identity from calling `.../take-custody` -- it has no special protection -- but doing so deletes this registrar's ability to sign any further create attestation on its domain ([REQ-7-9](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-7-9)); it has to keep a key this registrar can read for that.

**Rotating or taking custody of a key breaks that identity's entries in anything it guards, not just its log.** `.../rotate` and `.../take-custody` both replace the identity's `keys` -- but every ward whose `guardians` already names this identity recorded its keys as they were at that moment ([REQ-6-2](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-2)), and REQ-10-6/10-7's standing check compares against that snapshot. Neither endpoint touches any other identity's log, so the guardian loses standing to approve anything for every ward it guards the moment either one succeeds. `updateGuardian` ([REQ-7-15](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-7-15)) is how a ward re-seats a stale entry with the guardian's current keys -- approvable with the guardian's old and new keys together, no other guardian needed -- but only while the OLD key can still sign, which means re-seating every guarded ward has to happen *before* rotating or taking custody, not after. `.../rotate`'s new key is generated server-side and only revealed once rotation has already completed, so there's no way to pre-sign anything with it in advance; `.../take-custody`'s new key is the caller's own, known ahead of time, so re-seating first (signing each ward's `updateGuardian` with the old key via `.../pending/<id>/sign-as-self` and the new key locally) is the only order that actually works.

## 3. Asynchronous signature collection (`pending_proofs`)

For anything needing more than one proof collected over more than one request -- `addGuardian` (it always needs both the ward's own key and the incoming guardian's, two different parties, even for the very first guardian), `removeGuardian` against a guardian set that already has more than one member, `setPolicy`, `updateGuardian`, or a recovery/deactivation whose required guardians aren't all held by (or available in the same call to) this registrar.

There's no state machine. A proposal is a candidate operation (its `prev` already fixed against the current log) plus a growing array of proofs. Each proof secures the operation independently ([REQ-5-10](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-5-10)), so signers never need to see each other's proofs or coordinate at all -- they just add their own, in any order, whenever they get to it. After every addition, this registrar checks whether the proofs collected so far are now enough (exactly [REQ-10-5](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-5), the same check `.../operations` runs); if so, it submits the operation itself and the proposal is gone. If not, it keeps collecting.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `.../propose` | starts a proposal -- body `{operation, proof}`, where `operation` is the candidate without its `proof` member and `proof` is the proposer's own, over that same content. Returns `{status: "finalized", operation}` if that one proof was already enough, or `{status: "collecting", id, reason}` (the id to collect more against) otherwise |
| `POST` | `.../pending/<id>/sign` | a required signer adds their own proof -- body `{proof}`, over the same operation `GET .../pending/<id>` returns. Same two possible outcomes as `.../propose` |
| `POST` | `.../pending/<id>/sign-as-self` | `gw_session`-gated: signs server-side with the key this registrar already holds for the logged-in identity, same model as `.../rotate` |
| `POST` | `.../pending/<id>/withdraw` | cancels the proposal outright -- only the identity the proposal's log belongs to may do this, `gw_session`-gated |
| `GET` | `.../pending/<id>` | content-negotiated: `Accept: text/html` renders the browser page below; anything else returns `{did, operation, proofs, expiresAt}` |
| `GET` | `/api/me/pending-signatures` | every proposal currently collecting on the caller's log -- not proposals elsewhere the caller is a required signer for (e.g. as a guardian on a different identity); nothing yet surfaces those anywhere, the account dashboard (§8) included |

A proposal not satisfied within 7 days is removed by a daily sweep -- always a failure, never an automatic pass. There's no decline: a guardian who disagrees with a proposal simply never contributes a proof, which lets it expire on its own; nothing short of the proposal's target identity can remove it early.

**The browser page** (`GET .../pending/<id>` with `Accept: text/html`) shows the operation and how many proofs it's collected, with a **Sign** button shown only when the viewer is authenticated (§5's `gw_session`) as an identity this registrar holds a key for -- a logged-out viewer instead sees a link to §5's login page. A page that performed an action on a bare `GET` could be triggered by an email client's link-prefetching scanner before a person ever reads a message linking here, so every action here is a real `POST` from a button click, never a link. A required signer still has to be told a proposal exists by some other channel -- there's no notification of any kind yet, email included.

## 4. Orphan handling

Entirely the method's rule now, not this registrar's policy choice. When a `removeGuardian` empties a ward's `guardians` ([REQ-6-10](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-10)), its `policy.orphan` says what happens next, applied automatically by every verifier the same way, as part of replaying the operation itself -- never a separate action this registrar takes afterward:

- **`"deactivate"`** (the default) -- the ward deactivates itself, right there, with no further operation needed.
- **`"independent"`** -- nothing happens; the ward simply has no guardians from then on.
- **`"successor"`** -- its `successor` entry is promoted to its sole guardian, and `successor` is cleared. [REQ-10-7](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-7) requires this registrar to check that the successor's entry still has standing before accepting the `removeGuardian` that triggers this -- the one piece of this that's actually a registrar-side check, not purely a replay rule.

A ward whose policy names `"successor"` but has no `successor` entry set, or the reverse, is invalid at the operation that would create that mismatch ([REQ-6-14](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-14)) -- this registrar never needs to reconcile the two separately.

An absent policy member takes the default in [REQ-6-11](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-11) -- this registrar has no separate configured default to fall back to instead, so two verifiers resolving the same unset field never disagree depending on which registrar they asked.

## 5. Login / OIDC

Two independent flows share the same underlying credential (`login_secret`) and the same `gw_session` cookie, for two different purposes:

- `/authorize`, `/token`, `/userinfo`, `/revoke`, `/oauth/register-client`, `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, `/.well-known/jwks.json` -- the OIDC relying-party flow, for a third-party application that wants to let someone sign in with their Guardian ID. See `packages/server/src/oidc.ts`.
- `GET`/`POST /guardian-login?return_to=<path>` -- this registrar's first-party login, for this registrar's own pages: §3's browser voting page, the account dashboard (§8), and the admin console (§14), each redirecting here when there's no active session. No client registration: it's just "sign in, then take me back to the same-origin path that sent me here" (`return_to` is restricted to a relative path -- no open redirect to an external target). See `votingPage.ts`.
- `POST /guardian-logout?return_to=<path>` -- ends the session: deletes the `login_sessions` row server-side (not just the cookie client-side, so the old session id can't be replayed) and clears the cookie. POST only, same reasoning as every other state-changing action here -- never a bare link a scanner could trigger. Linked from the account dashboard (§8).

Named `/guardian-login`/`/guardian-logout`, not the shorter `/login`/`/logout`, because a registrar is commonly deployed on a domain that already has its own, unrelated human-facing `/login` and `/logout`. Each still needs its wrangler route entry -- worth checking your own host application's routes before adding any new top-level path here, not just these two.

**A relying party's `login_hint` always takes precedence over an already-active session.** `/authorize` compares a normalized `login_hint` against the current session's name (the same normalization a login attempt itself goes through), and falls through to a login prompt -- pre-filled with the hint, same as having no session at all -- whenever they don't match, rather than silently proceeding as whoever happens to still be logged in.

**The bare-domain root identity logs in like any other identity**, once an operator has given it a credential (`ROOT_WARD_LOGIN_SECRET`, see the top-level README's self-hosting section) -- the name field on either login form accepts `_`, the bare registrar domain, `@<domain>`, or `_@<domain>`, all four resolving to the same identity. The last form matters in practice, not just for completeness: a relying party that forces a `name@domain` shape on its login form (Tailscale's custom-OIDC login does) leaves `_@<domain>` as the only way to reach the root identity through that form at all, since neither bare `_` nor bare `@<domain>` fits what the form demands. `normalizeLoginIdentifier` (login.ts) checks the *extracted* name against `"_"` rather than the raw, untrimmed input, so `_` survives having `@domain` sliced off after it, the same way any other identity's name does. No self-service recovery if this password is lost -- see the README's section on resetting it directly against `held_keys.login_secret_hash`.

**`login_secret` can be either generated or user-chosen.** `POST /register` and this registrar's registration page both offer a choice: let the registrar generate a high-entropy secret, or set a password instead (`{"name": "...", "password": "..."}` in the JSON body; a minimum length is enforced, no further composition rules). A generated secret is returned once, in the response, and never again; a chosen password is never echoed back, since the caller already knows it. `.../login-secret` (reissuing) takes the same optional `password` either way -- changing your own credential later works identically to setting it at registration.

### 5.1 Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591)

A relying party no longer needs this registrar's operator to hand-insert an `oidc_clients` row -- `POST /oauth/register-client` is open, unauthenticated self-service, the same posture every other registration endpoint here already has:

```json {linenos=false}
{ "redirect_uris": ["https://app.example.com/callback"], "client_name": "Example App", "token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_basic" }
```

Returns `client_id` (and `client_secret`, unless `token_endpoint_auth_method` was `"none"` -- a public client, e.g. a mobile app or SPA, which authenticates with PKCE alone), plus a `registration_access_token` for `GET /oauth/register-client/<client_id>` (RFC 7592's read operation; update/delete aren't implemented yet). Both the issued `client_secret` and `registration_access_token` are shown exactly once, at registration time, the same convention every other one-time secret in this registrar already follows.

### 5.2 Consent

`/authorize` shows an "*App X* wants access to -- Allow/Deny" screen before issuing a code, remembered per `(ward, client_id)` so a returning user isn't re-asked unless the requested `scope` actually grows. Denying redirects back with `?error=access_denied` and no code, per RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1.

### 5.3 PKCE

Mandatory for every client, confidential or public -- the OAuth 2.1 baseline. `/authorize` refuses to issue a code at all without a `code_challenge` (`S256` only); `/token` treats a stored code somehow missing one as a bug, not a legitimate case to fall back on.

### 5.4 Tokens, refresh, and revocation

The `authorization_code` grant now always returns a `refresh_token` alongside the access/id tokens (`id`/`access` tokens: 1 hour; refresh tokens: 30 days). `grant_type=refresh_token` rotates on every use -- the presented token is marked spent and a new one issued in its place, sharing the same underlying "family." Presenting an already-rotated-away token again (something a legitimate client never does) is treated as evidence of theft: the entire family is revoked, not just the one request denied.

`POST /revoke` (RFC 7009) takes `{ token, token_type_hint? }`. A refresh token is revoked directly; an access/id token (otherwise a stateless, unrevokable JWT) has its `jti` added to a small blocklist that `/userinfo` checks going forward. Revocation is idempotent and always returns `200` regardless of whether the token was recognized, per RFC 7009 §2.2 -- never a way to probe which tokens exist.

Client authentication (where a client has a secret at all) accepts either `Authorization: Basic` or a `client_secret` body parameter, at both `/token` grant types.

### 5.5 `/userinfo` claims, and what's in the `id_token` itself

`/userinfo` always returns `sub`/`name`. `name` falls back to the bare registrar domain for the bare-domain root identity specifically, since its name is `""` (a sentinel, not a display name) and a literal empty string can fail a relying party's validation -- the same fallback `agentCard.ts` already uses for this identity's display name elsewhere. `email`/`email_verified` are included only when the access token's granted `scope` includes `email` *and* this identity has a verified forwarding address on file (§6) -- never invented, never returned for a scope that didn't ask for it. The root identity isn't excluded from this -- see §6's note on how it gets a verifiable email address despite having no name-shaped local part.

**`email`'s value is this ward's canonical `name@domain` -- never the forwarding address it happens to point mail at**, using `_` in place of a name for the bare-domain root specifically (§6). Those are two different facts: forwarding is where mail for this identity currently lands (an arbitrary, changeable third-party mailbox, never itself a second identity), while OIDC's `email` claim is supposed to assert something about *who the user is*. A relying party expecting its `login_hint` and the returned `email` to agree will otherwise see what looks like an identity mismatch, since the two addresses can differ by design. `email_verified: true` means this ward has confirmed, working forwarding configured (proof the identity is reachable by mail at all), not that the asserted `name@domain` address is itself a separately-verified mailbox. This also keeps a ward's actual forwarding destination private: it's this registrar's notification system's business alone, and a relying party asking for the `email` scope learns the Guardian ID being signed in with, never where that identity's mail happens to land today. No `email` claim at all when forwarding isn't configured.

**`email`/`email_verified`, when present, are also duplicated directly into the `id_token`**, not only reachable via a separate `/userinfo` call. This is a deliberate compatibility choice, not spec-mandated (OIDC allows claims to live in either place) -- plenty of real-world relying parties, especially simpler "generic OIDC" integrations, only ever decode the `id_token` and never make a second `/userinfo` round trip. Same exact condition and same shared helper as `/userinfo`'s check, not a duplicated logic path. Beyond those two claims, `id_token` stays minimal: `iss`, `sub` (the DID, not an email), `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `nonce`, `jti` -- a relying party that auto-matches incoming SSO identities against existing user records by email or username, rather than accepting a bare DID as the subject, may still need that identity invited/mapped manually on its side.

### 5.6 Finding the right registrar (discovery)

This is a client-side problem, not a missing endpoint -- a Guardian identifier already names its registrar (`domain:name`), so an RP's "Login with Guardian" button just needs to turn a person's `alice@acme.com`-shaped input into that domain's `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, then redirect through the ordinary flow above. A minimal reference implementation:

```js {linenos=false}
async function loginWithGuardian(identifier, redirectUri) {
  const [name, domain] = identifier.split("@");
  const discovery = await fetch(`https://${domain}/.well-known/openid-configuration`).then((r) => r.json());
  const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
  const challenge = base64url(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)));
  sessionStorage.setItem("guardian_code_verifier", verifier); // survives the redirect round-trip
  const url = new URL(discovery.authorization_endpoint);
  url.search = new URLSearchParams({
    client_id: MY_CLIENT_ID, redirect_uri: redirectUri, response_type: "code",
    scope: "openid", code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: "S256", login_hint: name,
  });
  location.href = url.toString();
}
```

`login_hint` (the standard OIDC authentication request parameter, already handled by `/authorize`) carries just the name part through to the registrar's login form -- the person never has to type the domain part twice in two different shapes.

## 6. Email forwarding

`POST .../email` (set up forwarding), `GET /verify-email` (confirm a forwarding address). See `packages/server/src/email.ts`.

**The bare-domain root identity uses `_` as its reserved local part** (the same convention §5's login already uses) -- `_@<domain>` both addresses mail to it and is the value `email.ts` writes into `email_forwarding`, so inbound routing (name-keyed at the local part, per `handleEmail`) can find it the same way it finds any named identity. This section's `.../email` endpoint still rejects root outright, though (no name to put in the path) -- root sets up forwarding through `/account/email` instead (§8), the one difference from how a named identity does it. Once set up, its OIDC `email` claim becomes `_@<domain>`, verifiable like any other -- which also means root can now satisfy a relying party that hard-requires an `email` claim (§5.5), something it had no way to do before this existed.

Outbound sending (the verification link itself) goes through `emailProviders.ts`. This registrar's choice of provider is a deployment config, not a protocol or method detail: `EMAIL_PROVIDER` (a `wrangler.jsonc` var) names one of `mailchannels` | `resend` | `cloudflare-native` | `log` (dev-only -- prints instead of sending). Nothing here is specific to this provider list -- adding another is one more small function, never a reason to touch any caller. Unconfigured, outbound sending fails with a clear configuration error rather than a vendor-specific HTTP status.

Every provider except one is a plain `(apiKey, opts) -> Response` function using only `fetch`, no Workers-specific API, and that provider's API key is set as a matching secret (`MAILCHANNELS_API_KEY`/`RESEND_API_KEY`) -- a self-hoster not on Cloudflare, or who'd rather not depend on a Workers-specific feature, picks one of these. `cloudflare-native` is the deliberate exception: Cloudflare's native Email Sending binding (`send_email` in `wrangler.jsonc`), needing no external account or API key at all, just `wrangler email sending enable <domain>` once per domain (Cloudflare then manages the SPF/DKIM records itself) and the Workers Paid plan. guardianspec.org, the live instance this spec documents, uses it.

## 7. Login secret

`POST .../login-secret` (reissue a lost or leaked one). See `packages/server/src/profile.ts`'s `reissueLoginSecret`.

## 8. Account dashboard

Everything above this point is an API, consumed by a relying party's code or an email client's link -- `GET /account` (after `/guardian-login`) is the one page where a person looks at and manages their own identity directly, the same first-party-HTML-page pattern §3's browser page already established. See `packages/server/src/accountPage.ts`.

Shows identity status, current guardians and successor with the identity's policy, the full activity log, anything still waiting on this identity's signature (its proposals collecting against its log, linked to §3's browser page), and every connected OAuth app (§5.2's consent records) with a "Revoke access" button that also kills any live refresh tokens for that app, not just the consent record -- revoking actually revokes, not just "stop remembering." A "Log out" button (§5's `POST /guardian-logout`) sits at the top.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/account` | the dashboard itself |
| `POST` | `/account/rotate` | rotate the identity's key |
| `POST` | `/account/login-secret/reissue` | reissue the login secret (a generated one, shown once, same convention every other one-time secret here follows) -- or, given `password`/`password_confirm` fields instead, set your own password |
| `POST` | `/account/email` | set up forwarding (§6) |
| `GET`/`POST` | `/account/tombstone` | a confirmation page -- requires typing the account's name, not a bare button -- then deactivates |
| `POST` | `/account/consents/revoke` | revoke a connected app's access |

A guardian steps down under its authority, not the ward's -- see `.../remove-self` (§2) or the generic multi-signer path (§3), not this dashboard, for that.
