Every action here, including email forwarding, works for the domain's bare-domain root identity too, the same as any named identity, once an operator has given it a login credential (see the top-level README's self-hosting section) -- root uses `_` as its reserved local part for forwarding (§6), the same convention §5's login already established for it.

## 9. Managed Identity API

This section is under revision -- a possible change to how `POST /register` names an initial guardian is awaiting a decision. **What's settled**: the guardian is derived from a validated access token's `sub`, never a client-supplied field -- `POST /register` with `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` and a token whose own granted `scope` includes `create:managed-identity` identifies who's consenting to become a guardian. A request with no bearer token at all gets the ordinary case: self-service, no guardian. A bearer token present but missing the scope is rejected outright (`403`). **What's under revision**: how the guardian relationship from that consent actually gets established in the new identity's log.

A platform wanting to use this needs its OIDC client (§5.1) and a token for the acting human carrying `create:managed-identity` -- normally obtained the same way any other scope is, through that human's `/authorize` consent. A client that only ever needs this occasionally can request it alongside `openid` at ordinary login time, store the resulting refresh token (§5.4), and mint a fresh access token on demand rather than redirecting through a fresh interactive consent on every single creation.

**The guardian's identity doesn't have to live on this same registrar.** A platform may legitimately onboard a human whose did:guardian identity is hosted elsewhere entirely -- their access token is then issued by *that* registrar, not this one, and a registrar can only verify a JWT signed with a key it actually holds. `FEDERATED_TRUSTED_ISSUERS` (an operator-configured, comma-separated allowlist of other registrar domains) opts this in explicitly: an access token whose `iss` matches a trusted peer is verified against *that peer's* `/.well-known/jwks.json` (fetched fresh, matched by `kid`), never assumed valid just because it claims a trusted domain. An issuer that's neither this registrar itself nor an explicitly trusted peer is rejected outright -- closed by default, the same posture every other access-control decision in this spec takes. `jti`-based revocation (§5.4) is only checked for this registrar's tokens; a federated peer's revocation state isn't visible here, the same limitation any JWT-based federation has without a shared introspection endpoint, bounded by the token's short TTL.

## 10. Delegation-chain tokens (token exchange)

A managed identity (§9) often needs to be *acted as* later, not just created once -- a platform letting its user operate an agent it guards, say. `POST /token` with `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange` (RFC 8693) mints a token whose `sub` is a target identity (`resource`, a DID this registrar custodies), given a `subject_token` (the caller's existing access token) proving who's actually asking:

```text {linenos=false}
POST /token
{
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange",
  "subject_token": "<the caller's access token>",
  "resource": "did:guardian:acme.com:some-agent",
  "client_id": "...", "client_secret": "..."
}
```

**Authorization checks `resource`'s current state directly.** The caller (the `subject_token`'s `sub`) must be `resource` itself, or named in `resource`'s current `guardians` or `successor`, resolved fresh from `resource`'s log every time -- never a cross-log liveness check, since verifying a log depends only on that log ([REQ-8-2](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-8-2)). Not a guardian, or not the identity itself: `403`. `resource` naming an identity this registrar doesn't hold a key for fails too -- there's no key material to issue a token for it.

**The issued token carries `sub` = the target, and `act: { sub: <the caller's DID> }`** -- the emerging OpenID on-behalf-of shape (`sub`/`act`), not a one-off: anything already built against that draft recognizes a token from this registrar unmodified. No `id_token` -- this isn't a fresh authentication event, just a scoped delegation of an already-authenticated caller's own, separately-proven authority. No refresh token either; the original `subject_token`'s session is what covers re-exchange later.

## 11. A2A (Agent2Agent) interop

A2A's Agent Card -- a JSON manifest advertising an identity's capabilities and how to authenticate with it -- is conventionally served at one fixed path per origin (`/.well-known/agent-card.json`), which doesn't fit this registrar's multi-tenant shape: many identities under one domain. The fixed path stays correct for a single-agent origin; a still-individual-draft WebFinger discovery profile (`draft-zhao-a2a-webfinger-00`) covers exactly the multi-tenant case -- WebFinger is the discovery layer that resolves a *named* identity to wherever its card actually lives, which doesn't have to be that fixed path.

- `GET /.well-known/agent-card.json` -- this domain's bare-domain root identity (its path segment is `_`, per the formal spec's [§4](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#4-identifier)), satisfying A2A's fixed-path convention for the one identity it actually fits here.
- `GET /.well-known/guardian/<name>/agent-card.json` -- a named identity's card, at a path consistent with every other resolution this registrar already does.
- `GET /.well-known/webfinger?resource=acct:<name>@<domain>` -- resolves a named identity to its card's URL (the JRD shape `draft-zhao-a2a-webfinger-00` itself specifies: `rel: "self"`, `type: "application/a2a+json"`).

Every card here declares `securitySchemes.oidc` (an `OpenIdConnectSecurityScheme` pointing at this registrar's `/.well-known/openid-configuration`) -- how an A2A client authenticates with this identity is just this registrar's OIDC flow, already documented in full above.

**The same WebFinger endpoint also serves OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0's unrelated WebFinger usage** -- `rel=http://openid.net/specs/connect/1.0/issuer` -- which is what a relying party that only has a user's identifier calls first, before ever fetching `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (e.g. a "log in with your identity provider" flow that takes `alice@guardianspec.org` directly, which is how Tailscale's custom-OIDC login discovers an issuer). The `href` returned is always the registrar's bare domain -- there's one OIDC issuer per registrar, not one per ward, so this step only ever confirms the identifier exists here at all. `rel` is a filter per RFC 7033: pass it zero or more times to get only matching links, or omit it to get every link this registrar knows for that resource (both the A2A one and the OIDC one, together).

**Deliberately unsigned in this pass.** A2A's `AgentCardSignature` (JWS, canonicalized) is optional, not required -- plain HTTPS already gives a verifier a weaker binding to this domain. Signing with a ward's own key (already custodied here, already published in its DID Document) is a natural fit for later, not something this first pass needed to block on.

## 12. Resource Indicators (planned MCP interop)

MCP's authorization spec is OAuth 2.1 plus mandatory Resource Indicators (RFC 8707) -- an MCP client treats the tool server it's calling as a *resource*, discovers who issues tokens for it, and asks for a token scoped to that one resource specifically, not a generic token good for anything the OAuth client happens to be. This registrar implements the two RFCs that mechanism needs, below -- but there is no MCP-specific integration yet (no tool-server registration, nothing validated against a real MCP client), so treat this section as what's needed for MCP interop, not MCP interop itself.

**`GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`** (RFC 9728, Protected Resource Metadata): this registrar is both its own authorization server and, for endpoints like `/userinfo`, a protected resource in its own right. The document names itself as both:

```json {linenos=false}
{
  "resource": "https://acme.com",
  "authorization_servers": ["https://acme.com"],
  "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"],
  "scopes_supported": ["openid", "email", "create:managed-identity"]
}
```

A `401` from `/userinfo` (missing, invalid, expired, or revoked token) carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://acme.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"` header (RFC 9728 §5.1) -- a generic client discovers the authorization server from the 401 alone, with nothing hardcoded out of band.

**`resource` at `/authorize` and `/token`** (RFC 8707 Resource Indicators): a client naming a `resource` (an absolute URI, no fragment -- e.g. the MCP tool server's URL) at `/authorize` gets an access token whose `aud` is that URI instead of the OAuth client's `client_id` -- the resource server checks a token meant for *it*, not evidence that *some* client authenticated. A refresh request may narrow which resource a fresh token is scoped to, but never introduce one that wasn't already established at the original `/authorize` -- a client that never asked for resource scoping can't add it later through refresh alone.

## 13. Cross-registrar signature relay

A guardian whose key is held by a *different* registrar than the one collecting a proposal can't produce a raw signature themselves -- their private key lives server-side on their own registrar and is never exposed to them. `GET`/`POST /relay-sign` lets them review and sign anyway, from their own registrar, using the key it holds for them.

`GET /relay-sign?domain=<proposal's registrar domain>&op=<pending id>`, `gw_session`-gated: fetches the operation's current status live from `GET https://<domain>/.well-known/guardian/pending/<op>` (the same no-auth, read-only endpoint §3 already documents) and shows it for review -- the operation type, how many proofs it's collected, and the full operation content.

`POST /relay-sign` (same `domain`/`op`, as form fields), re-fetches the same status fresh -- nothing from the `GET` is trusted -- then signs with the key this registrar holds for the logged-in identity and submits the result (`{proof}`) to `POST https://<domain>/.well-known/guardian/pending/<op>/sign`. That endpoint's proof check is unchanged: a stale or buggy relay page can fail a submission, never cause a wrongly-accepted operation.

There's no notification of a cross-registrar signature being needed, and no local record of one once it's been signed -- the same "nothing proactive yet" state §3 is in. Whoever's collecting the proposal has to tell the required signer where to go by some other channel.

## 14. Registration modes and the admin console

This registrar's public instance (guardianspec.org) runs **open**: anyone can `POST /register` and create an account. A different operator -- someone who controls the whole domain, personally or as a business, and wants their own root identity usable everywhere did:guardian is accepted, without exposing that same open door publicly -- instead runs **closed** (`REGISTRATION_MODE=closed`, a `vars` entry in `wrangler.jsonc`, not a secret).

Closed mode blocks only *anonymous* self-service at `/register` -- a bare name with no prior authorization, at all three of its branches (the browser form, the JSON API without a bearer token, and the registration page itself, which shows a plain "registration is closed" message instead of the form). A Managed Identity API bearer token (§9, `create:managed-identity` scope) still works either way, since that caller is already authenticated by a scope-checked token -- in a closed deployment such a token could only ever have come from someone who already has an account there, i.e. one the operator created.

**The admin console** (`GET /admin`, `GET`/`POST /admin/create-account`) is how a closed deployment's operator creates those accounts -- for other people or for agents they manage. Available on every deployment regardless of `REGISTRATION_MODE`; gated to a `gw_session` resolved to the root identity specifically (the identity with no name at all), and `ROOT_WARD_LOGIN_SECRET` (README.md) -- no separate role or permission system.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/admin` | lists every account on this registrar (name, DID, created-at) |
| `GET`/`POST` | `/admin/create-account` | the same generated-secret-or-set-your-own-password choice `/register` offers, no initial guardian -- add one afterward the same way a self-service registration would |
| `GET` | `/admin/apps` | lists every OAuth/OIDC client ("app") dynamically registered against this registrar's provider (§5) |
| `GET`/`POST` | `/admin/apps/new` | register a new OAuth client by hand, as an alternative to dynamic client registration (`POST /oauth/register-client`) -- name plus one or more redirect URIs |
| `POST` | `/admin/apps/<client_id>/delete` | revokes that client's registration entirely |

**v1 scope.** The admin console lists and creates; it doesn't let the root identity view, rotate, or deactivate *someone else's* account -- a bigger question (impersonation/management scope) left for its future discussion. No claim-link credential flow -- an admin-created account's owner changes their password any time afterward through the ordinary account dashboard (§8), the same action available to any self-registered account.

## Changelog

This draft replaces all earlier drafts of this document. Earlier drafts are in the repository history.

Fixes made while integrating this registrar with third-party OIDC relying parties (Tailscale's custom-OIDC login, specifically), kept here rather than narrated inline in the sections above:

- `/authorize` previously let an already-active session from a different login silently continue into a new relying-party flow, with no check against what that flow actually requested -- surfaced as a confusing identity-mismatch error on the relying party's side. Fixed by comparing `login_hint` against the current session (§5).
- `normalizeLoginIdentifier` checked the raw login input against `"_"` instead of the name extracted after slicing off `@domain`, so `_@<domain>` -- the only login form some relying parties' own forms allow for the root identity -- didn't resolve. Fixed (§5).
- `/userinfo`'s `name` claim returned a literal empty string for the root identity, which failed at least one relying party's validation. Fixed with the same domain fallback `agentCard.ts` already used elsewhere (§5.5).
- The `email` claim originally asserted a ward's forwarding destination instead of its canonical `name@domain` address, which both leaked where a ward's mail actually lands and caused a genuine identity-mismatch failure at a relying party that cross-checked `login_hint` against the returned `email`. Fixed (§5.5).
- WebFinger (§11) never applied the `_` -> `""` translation every other root-identity path already used, so `acct:_@<domain>` 404'd. Fixed.

# Prior art and comparisons

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/prior-art/

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "TechArticle",
  "headline": "Prior art and comparisons",
  "description": "How did:guardian relates to did:webvh, did:plc, KERI's delegated AIDs, the Sovrin Guardianship Task Force's work, and ERC-4337 social recovery -- and when one of those fits better.",
  "url": "https://guardianspec.org/docs/prior-art/",
  "about": { "@type": "SoftwareSourceCode", "name": "did:guardian", "codeRepository": "https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian", "programmingLanguage": "TypeScript" }
}
</script>

did:guardian's contribution is group guardianship as a first-class part of a DID method: a configurable group of other identities, with changeable membership, that can recover a lost key, remove itself, or deactivate a ward, verified the same way any other operation in the method's log is. Five other projects cover related ground, each from a different angle. None of them do exactly this; some do something better for a narrower need.

## did:webvh

[did:webvh](https://identity.foundation/didwebvh/v1.0/) ("did:web with Verifiable History", formerly did:tdw) extends `did:web` with a self-certifying identifier, a verifiable hash-chained history of every DID document version, pre-rotation (committing to the next key's hash in advance, so a compromised current key can't redirect control to an attacker-chosen one), and optional third-party witnesses who attest they observed an update.

**Comparable:** witnesses are a multi-party mechanism, closer in shape than most of the others here to did:guardian's group concept.

**Different:** a witness attests that an update happened; it has no authority to make one. did:webvh has no concept of a group that can recover, revoke, or act on behalf of the identity -- control stays with whoever holds the (pre-rotated) key, full stop. If you need a tamper-evident document history and nothing more -- no recovery path if the key is lost, no standing oversight -- did:webvh is a lighter-weight fit than did:guardian for exactly that. did:webvh's identifier is also self-certifying and portable in a way did:guardian's isn't: a did:webvh identifier can move to a new location (its own `#updateDomain` mechanism) without losing its identity, since the identifier's own hash is what anchors trust, not where it currently resolves. A did:guardian identifier names its domain directly (formal spec [§4](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#4-identifier)) and stays bound to it for the identifier's own life, with "link, don't move" (a new identifier plus mutual `alsoKnownAs`) as the documented alternative to migration.

## did:plc

[did:plc](https://github.com/did-method-plc/did-method-plc) (Bluesky/AT Protocol's method) is the closest structural relative here: an append-only operation log, replayed to derive current state, with a two-tier key model (a rotation-key set and an operational key) -- did:guardian's own operation log and replay model are the same shape.

**Comparable:** the log/replay mechanics are close enough that did:guardian is best understood as did:plc's model plus group guardianship, not a wholly separate design. did:plc also lets a rotation key undo a recent, unauthorized rotation within a recovery window; did:guardian has no equivalent -- an accepted operation is permanent, and recovering from a compromised key means the guardians rotate forward to a new one, never rolling one back.

**Different:** did:plc's rotation-key tier is a single, ordered list of keys -- whichever one, in order, is willing and able to sign, authorizes recovery. did:guardian's guardian tier is a configurable, unordered M-of-N group of other identities instead -- each one controlled by whoever or whatever its own owner chooses (a person, a committee, another identity entirely), not a second key one party happens to hold. did:plc is also directory-resolved (a single, centrally-operated PLC directory); did:guardian follows `did:web`'s own domain-scoped resolution instead, any number of independent registrars rather than one shared directory.

## KERI delegated AIDs

In [KERI](https://trustoverip.github.io/kswg-keri-specification/), a delegated identifier is established through mutual, cooperative seals -- both the delegator and the delegate cryptographically commit in their own key event logs, so neither can unilaterally impose or dissolve the relationship. Delegation composes recursively into trees (a root authority delegating to several others, each of those delegating further).

**Comparable:** the mutual-consent requirement is philosophically close to did:guardian's "guardianship is explicit and consensual."

**Different:** KERI delegation is structurally delegator-to-delegate, not a configurable M-of-N peer group. There's no native concept of several guardians, with changeable membership, jointly overseeing one identity under a threshold -- nesting builds a hierarchy, not a flat guardian set. A guardian can itself have its own guardians in did:guardian too (a guardian is just an identity, REQ-6-2), so a chain of relationships can still form -- but each one is a separate, flat M-of-N group, not a single structured delegation hierarchy with KERI's own authority semantics. If that structured chain is the actual shape you need, KERI's delegation model fits it directly.

## The Sovrin Guardianship Task Force

Sovrin's Guardianship Task Force published whitepapers (2019, a revised v2 in 2023) modeling guardianship -- specifically for people who can't act for themselves: children, people with cognitive disabilities, refugees without personal devices -- using **W3C Verifiable Credentials** issued on top of an existing DID method (`did:sov`/`did:indy`).

**Comparable:** of everything here, this is the closest in motivation -- it's explicitly about guardianship for people who need someone else able to act on their behalf, the same case did:guardian is built around.

**Different:** a guardianship credential is revocable and verifiable as a credential, but the underlying DID method has no native awareness of it -- enforcing it is up to whatever application checks the credential, not the method's resolution or operation log. If guardianship needs scoping per relationship into fine-grained categories (medical decisions, financial decisions, digital-account access, each a separate issuable credential type), a verifiable-credential layer like this is more flexible than did:guardian's single, uniform, method-level relationship -- did:guardian doesn't distinguish *what kind* of authority a guardian holds, only how many of them need to agree.

## ERC-4337 social recovery wallets

Ethereum's account abstraction standard lets a smart-contract wallet designate other addresses as guardians, with an M-of-N threshold of their approval able to replace the wallet's controlling key -- logic that lives in the contract, increasingly modularized under ERC-7579.

**Comparable:** the M-of-N guardian-set mechanic is structurally close to did:guardian's own `policy.recovery`/`policy.removal` settings.

**Different:** ERC-4337's guardian logic lives entirely at the smart-contract/application layer, tied to one chain's execution environment, not in did:guardian's own method-level operation log -- a DID layered on top of such a wallet wouldn't inherit guardianship as a property of the DID method itself the way a did:guardian identity does. If the identity in question *is* a crypto wallet, and on-chain enforcement of recovery logic matters more than portability across chains or off-chain use, ERC-4337's own pattern fits that directly.

## When did:guardian fits, and when it doesn't

did:guardian fits when guardianship needs to be a property of the identity -- verifiable by replaying a log, with no dependency on a specific credential issuer, smart contract platform, or application staying alive to enforce it. It doesn't fit as well when you need a self-certifying, portable identifier instead of a domain-bound one (did:webvh), a single ordered recovery-key list with no group concept (did:plc), hierarchical delegation (KERI), fine-grained per-relationship authority types (a verifiable-credential layer), or on-chain enforcement tied to one execution environment (ERC-4337).


---

# Get Started

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/how-to/

For an introduction to the method, see the [guide](/docs/) first -- this page assumes you already know what a ward and a guardian are, and gets straight to running things.

## Quickstart

Create an identity, resolve it, and add a guardian, using [`@did-guardian/cli`](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/tree/main/packages/cli):

```text {linenos=false}
npm install -g @did-guardian/cli
```

**Create an identity:**

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian register alice --registrar guardianspec.org
```

```text {linenos=false}
Created did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice

Login secret (shown once -- save it now, there's no recovery path if you lose it):
<secret>
```

**Resolve it.** No authentication needed -- this works for anyone, anywhere:

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian resolve did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice
```

```text {linenos=false}
First resolution of did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice -- pinned anchor <anchor>.
{ "...": "an ordinary W3C DID Core document" }
```

That pin is the CLI's own record that this is the same `alice` it saw before -- a later resolution with a different anchor gets reported loudly, not silently accepted.

**Add a guardian.** Register a second identity for whoever's becoming the guardian, log in as them, and adopt -- two steps, each its own identity:

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian register bob --registrar guardianspec.org
did-guardian login did:guardian:guardianspec.org:bob --login-secret <bob's secret>
did-guardian guardian adopt did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice
```

That prints a pending id. Whoever controls `alice` (here, the same person, for this walkthrough) logs in as `alice` and finishes it:

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian login did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice --login-secret <alice's secret>
did-guardian guardian confirm-adopt did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice <pending id>
```

A guardian relationship exists only once both sides have signed for it -- `bob`'s own consent to take on the role, and `alice`'s own approval of `bob` as its guardian.

Every command above has a plain HTTP equivalent too -- see the [registrar API doc](/docs/registrar/) for the exact requests, or point the CLI through a local HTTP proxy to see exactly what it sent and got back. `register` and `resolve` also take `--json` directly, for a machine-readable response with no proxy needed.

### Holding a key yourself instead

Everything above leaves the registrar holding both keys, encrypted. If you'd rather hold a key yourself, log back in as `alice` specifically first -- the session above is `bob`'s, and `take-custody` acts as whichever identity is actually logged in, never the identity named in the command itself:

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian login did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice --login-secret <alice's secret>
did-guardian key take-custody did:guardian:guardianspec.org:alice
```

That `take-custody` command ends the registrar's custody of `alice`'s key for good -- `did-guardian guardian add`/`recover`/`deactivate` then sign and submit directly with keys you hold, no session needed. If `alice` is herself a guardian of some other ward, its own entry for her goes stale the moment this succeeds (it recorded her keys as they were when she was added) -- see the [registrar doc](/docs/registrar/#2-self-contained-convenience-endpoints) for why, and re-seat that entry with an `updateGuardian` *before* taking custody, not after.

For a brand-new identity, `did-guardian create <name> --registrar <domain>` builds a create operation with a key you generate yourself and never hand to any registrar, then submits it for real. `create <name> --domain <domain>` (no `--registrar`) builds the same operation fully offline instead, with no network call at all -- useful for understanding the mechanics or embedding [`@did-guardian/lib`](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/tree/main/packages/lib) directly, but the result is a draft until something actually accepts it.

See the CLI's README for the full command list, including `verify` (offline, §8 only) and `operation propose`/`operation sign` (the generic path for an operation needing more approvals than one command can produce).

## How-to guides

Each of these walks through one specific task, start to finish, with commands you can run directly.

- [Give an AI agent an identity a human can revoke](/docs/how-to/ai-agent-identity/)
- [Sign in via custom OIDC](/docs/how-to/custom-oidc-login/)
- [Self-host a registrar](/docs/how-to/self-host/)
- [Recover after a lost key](/docs/how-to/recover-lost-key/)


---

# Give an AI agent an identity a human can revoke

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/how-to/ai-agent-identity/

In did:guardian, an AI agent gets its own identity, with its own key. A human (or a team) becomes that agent's guardian -- a did:guardian group with the power to recover the agent's identity if its key is compromised, and to shut it down when it's retired. A conformant registrar can also let that guardian act as the agent for things it can't approve alone; the reference registrar does this through [delegation-chain token exchange](/docs/registrar/#10-delegation-chain-tokens-token-exchange), a registrar-profile feature, not something the did:guardian method itself defines.

By default, the reference registrar holds both the agent's key and the human guardian's key, encrypted, and produces whichever proof a command needs on their behalf. Neither recovery nor shutdown requires the guardian to personally hold or see the agent's key. As long as the registrar holds both keys, it can also act as either party for anything either could authorize alone -- taking custody of a key (covered below, under "Make a human its guardian") is what changes that.

Commands below use [`@did-guardian/cli`](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/tree/main/packages/cli) (`npm install -g @did-guardian/cli`); see the [registrar API doc](/docs/registrar/) for the plain HTTP underneath any of them.

## Register the agent's identity

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian register support-bot-7 --registrar guardianspec.org
```

```text {linenos=false}
Created did:guardian:guardianspec.org:support-bot-7

Login secret (shown once -- save it now, there's no recovery path if you lose it):
<secret>
```

Store that secret with the agent's own operator, not with the human who's about to become its guardian -- the whole point of the next step is that the guardian shouldn't need it.

## Make a human its guardian

Adding a guardian is a signed operation on both sides -- the agent's own create carries no initial guardian, since establishing one needs that guardian's own signature, which a brand-new identity can't have collected yet. The human guardian needs a did:guardian identity too -- register one if they don't already have one:

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian register priya --registrar guardianspec.org
```

Then log in as the human and accept the agent as a ward:

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian login did:guardian:guardianspec.org:priya --login-secret <priya's secret>
did-guardian guardian adopt did:guardian:guardianspec.org:support-bot-7
```

That prints a pending id. Whoever controls the agent's own identity (its operator, holding the login secret from the step above) logs in as it and finishes the other half:

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian login did:guardian:guardianspec.org:support-bot-7 --login-secret <agent's secret>
did-guardian guardian confirm-adopt did:guardian:guardianspec.org:support-bot-7 <pending id>
```

Nobody outside the registrar ever sees either private key -- but in this default held mode, the registrar itself still can, since it's the one producing both proofs: it can sign as the agent, or as the human guardian, for any operation either of them could authorize alone, including recovering or deactivating the agent without the human's own session ever being involved. Taking custody of a key (below) is what actually removes the registrar from that part of the trust model, not merely not seeing the key afterward.

**If you'd rather hold a key yourself** for one or both parties -- the agent, say, if you don't want the registrar able to sign on its behalf at all -- `did-guardian key take-custody <did>` ends the registrar's custody of that identity's key, and `did-guardian guardian add <agent-did> <guardian-did> --ward-key <label> --guardian-key <label>` signs and submits the same guardian relationship directly, once both parties hold keys locally. Doing this before the guardian relationship exists, as above, is safe -- but taking custody of a key that already guards something else (a human running more than one agent, say) breaks that other relationship's own standing the moment it succeeds, since it was recorded with the old key; see the [registrar doc](/docs/registrar/#2-self-contained-convenience-endpoints) for why, and the fix.

## What the guardian can do afterward

**Recover it, if its key is lost or compromised.** A guardian-initiated `update`, signed with the guardian's key (never the agent's) -- see [Recover after a lost key](/docs/how-to/recover-lost-key/) for the exact steps; the same mechanics apply whether the ward is a person or an agent.

**Shut it down.**

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian guardian deactivate did:guardian:guardianspec.org:support-bot-7 did:guardian:guardianspec.org:priya --guardian-key <label> --submit
```

This works in one call whenever `policy.deactivation` lets a guardian approve alone (`by: "guardians"` or `"either"`, with `priya`'s own signature meeting `policy.deactivation.threshold`) -- the default policy (`by: "both"`) also needs the agent's own key, so with no change to policy this command reports what else is needed instead of succeeding; the generic multi-signer path (`did-guardian operation propose`/`operation sign`, [registrar API doc](/docs/registrar/) §3) collects whatever that turns out to be.

Either way this deactivates the agent's identity permanently -- its log stays public and readable, but no further operation on it is accepted. Registration always starts an identity on the default policy; if you want deactivation to need more than one guardian to agree, change `policy.deactivation` afterward with `setPolicy` (through the generic multi-signer path -- there's no dedicated command for it yet).

## Short-lived agents

A long-lived guardian managing a fleet of agents that come and go doesn't need a human name for each one -- a generated name like `"agent-$(openssl rand -hex 3)"` (or any generator producing a valid one) works fine. Each agent still needs its own `guardian add`/`guardian adopt`-`confirm-adopt` to establish the fleet's own guardian -- there's no way to name a guardian directly at creation.

Retiring one is the same `deactivate` described above, approved by the guardian. There's no bulk-retirement operation, each agent is deactivated individually. Names are never reused ([REQ-10-12](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-12)) and logs are never deleted ([REQ-10-11](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-10-11)), so a retired agent's full history stays resolvable forever, even deactivated -- a guardian's historical keys have to stay verifiable for as long as anything it ever signed might need checking, which means nothing it guarded can be deleted out from under that either. Running many short-lived agents through one registrar does mean that registrar's storage grows without bound; that's the cost of this design, not a bug to work around.


---

# Sign in via custom OIDC

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/how-to/custom-oidc-login/

The reference registrar runs as a standard OpenID Connect provider -- a registrar-profile feature, not something every conformant registrar has to offer. A relying party that accepts a custom or generic OIDC identity provider -- Tailscale, Grafana, and many self-hosted tools all have an option like this -- works against it the same way it would against any other provider.

## Register an OAuth client

Dynamic client registration ([RFC 7591](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591)) needs no prior account on the registrar:

```text {linenos=false}
curl -X POST https://guardianspec.org/oauth/register-client \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"redirect_uris": ["https://your-app.example.com/oauth/callback"], "client_name": "My App"}'
```

```json {linenos=false}
{
  "client_id": "...",
  "client_secret": "...",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://your-app.example.com/oauth/callback"],
  "client_name": "My App",
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_basic",
  "registration_access_token": "...",
  "registration_client_uri": "https://guardianspec.org/oauth/register-client/..."
}
```

Use `client_id` and `client_secret` wherever the relying party asks for them. The issuer is the registrar's domain (`https://guardianspec.org`); its discovery document is at the standard `/.well-known/openid-configuration` path.

## Prompt behavior

This registrar doesn't read the `prompt` parameter at all -- if the relying party's own setup screen asks which values to request, leave it unset or pick whichever it's happy with; none of them change what actually happens here. The flow it runs is always the same: show the login form if there's no existing `gw_session`, then show the consent page unless this client already has a recorded decision for the scope being requested.

## Signing in as the root identity

Some relying parties force a `name@domain` shape on their login field and never give a way to type a bare domain. If you're signing in as a registrar's bare-domain root identity rather than a named ward, `_@<your-domain>` is the one form that still gets through a form like that -- `_` is root's reserved local part everywhere a named ward would use its name.

## If the relying party validates claims strictly

A registrar's `id_token`/`userinfo` claims stay minimal and privacy-preserving: `email` (when the ward has verified forwarding set up) always asserts the ward's canonical Guardian-ID-based address, never wherever that mail actually forwards to. If a relying party's validation expects something a registrar doesn't assert by default, check the [registrar API doc](/docs/registrar/)'s section on `/userinfo` and the id_token for exactly what's included.


---

# Recover after a lost key

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/how-to/recover-lost-key/

Two separate cases share the name "recovery," and need different things.

**A backup key.** An identity can hold up to 8 keys at once ([REQ-6-1](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-1)). If `alice` still holds even one of hers, that one key alone can sign an `update` installing a fresh one -- no guardian needed at all. This is the simplest case, and worth setting up ahead of time: a second key, kept somewhere separate from the first, turns "lost a key" into an ordinary self-service rotation.

**Guardian-approved recovery**, this page's main topic: if `alice` has lost every key she held, enough of her guardians (meeting whatever `policy.recovery` sets, `majority` by default) can issue her a fresh one instead. The old key is never needed, and never recovered -- it's replaced. Without a backup key of her own and without a guardian, there's genuinely nothing that can help: did:guardian uses guardianship for this, deliberately, rather than `did:plc`'s ordered recovery-key list -- set one up (see below) before this happens, not after.

A held ward is a different case from either of these: the registrar still custodies the key behind it, so what's actually "lost" is usually just your own login credential, not the key itself -- that's an account-recovery problem (see [self-host](/docs/how-to/self-host/)'s own login flow), separate from this page's own guardian-signed `update`.

A did:guardian guardian doesn't have to be a separate person -- [REQ-6-2](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-2) makes a guardian an identity, which `alice` herself can control: a cold-storage identity (a key generated once, kept offline, and never used for anything else) named as `alice`'s own guardian covers the case where there's no one else to name, with no second party involved. Set one up while `alice` still holds a key herself -- `did-guardian create <name> --registrar <domain>` builds the cold-storage identity with its own self-held key (never `register`, which generates a registrar-held one, the opposite of what a cold-storage guardian needs), then add it as a guardian ([`guardian add`](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/tree/main/packages/cli), if both keys are self-held).

## The recovery itself

```text {linenos=false}
did-guardian guardian recover did:guardian:example.com:alice did:guardian:example.com:bob --guardian-key bob --submit
```

This `guardian recover` command needs `bob` (the guardian) to hold a key [`@did-guardian/cli`](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/tree/main/packages/cli) can sign with directly. With `--submit`, it sends the operation immediately and reports whether `alice`'s own `policy.recovery` was satisfied by bob's approval alone; without it, the command only prints what it built.

If bob's own key is still held by a registrar rather than local, don't run `key take-custody` to work around that -- bob's existing entry in `alice`'s own `guardians` list names bob's key as the registrar still custodies it, and taking custody changes that key out from under it, costing bob his standing to approve anything for `alice` at all (it would need its own `updateGuardian` to re-seat, which a sole, registrar-held guardian has no way to produce either). Use `did-guardian operation propose`/`did-guardian operation sign` instead: propose the operation, then have bob log in and approve the pending operation through his own account dashboard, where the registrar signs with the key it already holds for him, once he's reviewed and confirmed exactly what it's for. The same path covers more than one required guardian too, each signing in turn against the same pending id.

A fresh key is generated and saved automatically (as `<ward-did>-recovered`); pass `--new-key <label>` to install one you already hold instead.

## If the lost key was already used by whoever took it

A key that's lost to theft, not just misplaced, might already have been used to rotate the identity before a guardian ever gets involved. There's no way to undo that rotation -- an accepted operation is permanent, by design, so there's nothing for a guardian to point at and roll back. The same guardian-signed `update` above still works, and still replaces the compromised key; it just adds a new operation on top of the compromised one rather than erasing it. The compromised rotation stays visible in the identity's own history, for anyone who resolves it to see.

## After recovering

The ward's guardian set is untouched by this -- `update` only ever replaces keys, never guardianship. Nothing else needs to change.


---

# Self-host a registrar

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/how-to/self-host/

`packages/server` is a self-hostable registrar: `packages/lib` plus an HTTP surface, an OIDC/OAuth2.1 identity provider, an account dashboard, an admin console, and an agent-identity API. This project's public registrar, guardianspec.org, is exactly this code, deployed to Cloudflare Workers.

## Deploy

```bash {linenos=false}
git clone https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian
cd did-method-guardian/packages/server
npm install

# Create a D1 database, then fill its id into wrangler.jsonc's
# "database_id" (it ships as a placeholder, "REPLACE_ME").
npx wrangler d1 create guardian-server

npx wrangler d1 migrations apply guardian-server --remote

# AES-GCM key, base64, 32 bytes -- encrypts custodied private keys at rest.
npx wrangler secret put KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY

# Set REGISTRAR_DOMAIN in wrangler.jsonc's "vars" to your domain,
# then deploy.
npx wrangler deploy
```

That's a working registrar: anyone can `POST /register` and create an identity, OIDC endpoints are live, resolution works. A few things are opt-in from there, each documented inline in `wrangler.jsonc`'s comments:

- **Rate limiting** on `/register` and `/guardian-login` (a KV namespace -- without it, these endpoints simply have no rate limiting, rather than failing).
- **Outbound email** for forwarding and verification, either Cloudflare's native Email Sending binding or an external provider (MailChannels, Resend) via `EMAIL_PROVIDER` and an API key secret.
- **Federated trust** (`FEDERATED_TRUSTED_ISSUERS`) if you want this registrar to also accept another registrar's access tokens at bearer-token-gated endpoints.

## The bare-domain root identity

Every deployment has one identity with no name at all -- `did:guardian:<your-domain>`, created the first time anything else registers (never by a resolution, which only ever reads). It attests every other identity's own create operation and, once given a login credential, is a fully usable identity like any other.

```bash {linenos=false}
npx wrangler secret put ROOT_WARD_LOGIN_SECRET
```

Sign in with the name field left as `_`, your bare domain, `@your-domain`, or `_@your-domain` -- all four mean the same thing. There's no self-service recovery path for this one credential if you lose it; see [README.md](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/blob/main/README.md#self-hosting-the-bare-domain-root-identity) for the direct-database reset procedure.

## Open vs. closed registration

**Open** (the default, and how guardianspec.org runs): anyone can register. **Closed** (`REGISTRATION_MODE: "closed"` in `wrangler.jsonc`'s `vars`): public self-service is blocked, and the root identity creates accounts for specific people or agents instead, through the admin console (`/admin`, `/admin/create-account`) -- available on every deployment regardless of this setting, gated to a session authenticated as the root identity. This is the shape for an operator who controls the whole domain -- personally, or as a business -- and wants named accounts for their team or the agents they run, without an open door to the public.

Full environment-variable reference: [`packages/server/src/env.ts`](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/blob/main/packages/server/src/env.ts).
